speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-120, to amend the Income Tax Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think I need make no more than a very brief statement on this motion for second reading, because the bulk of the discussion on this bill will no doubt occur in the committee. I have already given the house notice of four amendments which will be introduced at the committee stage. I should like to mention one other that I am sure will greatly shorten the committee's labours.
One matter which has occupied a prominent place in the bill is a proposal to amend certain sections of the Income Tax Act in relation to personal corporations. To facilitate further study of the subject and the passage of this present measure, when we reach the committee stage I shall be proposing that the provisions of the bill in that regard be dropped. There have been some representations respecting this subject indicating that various groups would like further time to study the provisions in that regard; therefore I shall be proposing that they be eliminated from this bill. At the same time I shall be asking interested groups, the usual professional groups and others, to study these clauses and make their representations and suggestions based thereon after a careful study of the subject. Those representations will be welcomed and will be made use of in the future for the guidance of those concerned in considering proper legislative amendments affecting our present act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Clauses 23 and 24 of the bill. There are one or two incidental amendments which follow.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that these proposals will facilitate discussion of the bill. I may say the bill was introduced in the house a week ago. We have had the benefit of the usual conferences with representatives of the legal and accounting professions. We are always grateful to those groups for the assistance of their skilful examination of these legislative proposals and the benefit of discussion of them with such persons.
I think, Mr. Speaker, all other matters that are dealt with in the bill can more properly be discussed at the committee stage.

Mr. Speaker, the announcement just made by the Minister of Finance is something of a shocker, because when he introduced his budget resolutions on June 20 he indicated that among the considerations that had had most careful review were those that related to personal corporations. I would have assumed that because the amendments proposed in the bill before us relating to personal corporations cover many pages, the department would have given all the implications a great deal of study before bringing forward the amendments introduced on June 20.
In addition, we know that since June 20 the minister has announced three or four further amendments that will be before us when we are in committee today, all of them indicating changes of mind. But this one which involves many pages of this 36-page income tax bill apparently is the result of a decision that has been made over the week end. I say this is typical of the lack of preparation on the part of the government in the presentation of legislation to this session of parliament.
Apart from the very extensive legislation with respect to personal corporations, I take it that the amendments in the bill before us are chiefly concerned with proposals in respect of profit sharing plans. This, of course, is another matter upon which the government have delayed. They introduced a bill in 1960 and asked the public and those concerned to make comments upon the draft bill in the intervening period. We do not have a separate bill before us with respect to deferred profit sharing, but rather that matter is incorporated in amendments to the Income Tax Act this year. These appear to be desirable and acceptable, and a great many of the amendments in the bill appear to relate to changes consequent upon that decision. Apart from that, I must say that there is very little in the bill, lengthy though it is in text, that is argumentative.
I think the most significant thing is that in connection with incentives to industry, there is nothing in the bill particularly pinpointing incentives to exporters. In my opinion this is one place where anyone who was predicting

Income Tax Act
what the minister might do this year might well have been disappointed and, indeed, distressed.
We know that the government appointed a productivity council this year. We have heard very little from that council with the exception of some speeches that have been made by the chairman, but we know that the chairman has been emphasizing the necessity of giving special tax incentives to those engaged in the export industries. There is no provision here for those producing for external consumption that goes beyond the depreciation available to them as well as to producers for internal consumption, and which would appeal to us as satisfying the statement made by Mr. de Young in London, Ontario, on May 29, when he said that Canada should seriously consider adopting tax amendments that would provide incentives to our export industries on a basis comparable with what we know is enjoyed by our competitors in other parts of the world, particularly in western Europe. What is the purpose of setting up this new organization, the national productivity council, if this government in a long delayed budget is not going to take advantage of advice of this kind, which is among the immediate advice that so far has been made public arising from the setting up of the council?
In addition, we had a valuable study in a committee of the other place. I refer to the special Senate committee on manpower and employment. In a summary of their long and excellent work they place very heavy emphasis upon the importance of taxation incentives, in particular to encourage exports. I refer to page 5 of the report, where the following is found:
Because of the immediate importance of such a new emphasis in industrial policy urgent consideration should be given to the possibility of establishing effective and practicable tax reliefs or tax incentives for the achievement of increases in the export of manufactured goods.
This government in its budget, rather than adopting a pinpointing effort such as has been prominently suggested for a long time particularly for export industries, has decided that its chief instrument in this field will be the exchange control fund. What have we to lose by giving special tax concessions to the export industries such as were suggested last year by the Leader of the Opposition, such as have been suggested by the Senate committee on manpower and employment, and such as have been suggested by the national productivity council? What have we to lose if the tax concessions relate simply to an increase in exports, something we have not experienced in the previous tax year?
In my criticism following the presentation of the budget on June 20 I indicated that we

had had an instrument that had proven successful in the expansion of our resource industries, namely a three year tax exemption applicable to industries that were to be established. What have we to lose in this kind of incentive if we are encouraging industry that has paid no tax up to now and has received no encouragement to become established?
In his budget speech the minister referred to the depreciation allowances that were to be provided to the so-called depressed areas under the terms of his baby budget. I remind hon. members of the house of the comment published by the Financial Post to the effect that this did not involve very much incentive. Hon. members will remember the pertinent statement that it was felt that the only labour that was likely to be created by anything as insignificant as the incentives involved in the baby budget would be labour created in the civil service in connection with the examination of depreciation allowances of this highly involved and complex type offered to new industry.
In the recent budget an increase was made in the depreciation allowances extended to persons who are investing in machinery and equipment beyond their norm and beyond what they did last year. I commend the minister for that. In addition, special advantages are now allowed to encourage research. Again I commend the minister for that. However, I say this. After so many people seem to agree almost universally that some very carefully directed incentives should be provided to those who might increase their exports, to me it is very striking and very distressing to find in the budget no reference to this matter. Having regard to the very well known activities of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this field in recent months, this omission indicates to me that he apparently lost a fight with the Minister of Finance-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no fight.

-in cabinet. The Minister of Finance, facing a deficit, apparently won in the desire to hang on to dollars in tax revenues and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has wanted to increase exports from this country, has apparently lost in that internal fight. I say this is very significant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no fight.

The minister then, in so far as export industries are concerned, is depending simply on what I call the main item of his budget, namely his decision to flip flop and somersault; to say that what he said

Income Tax Act
last year was invalid; and to say that this year the proper thing is to gamble or speculate on the exchange fund and to depreciate the Canadian dollar, and that this is a policy to be preferred to that of some special tax incentives to the export industries.
I say that again we are in the dark. Last week's press indicated that this agency of the Minister of Finance, namely the exchange fund, seemingly is not operating in a complete spirit of harmony with the language of the budget when the minister said he wanted the dollar to go to a significant discount. There is evidence that the administration is doing the very opposite, that it is trying to prevent the dollar from going to a significant discount, and that it is using the funds of the exchange control board for that purpose. Inasmuch as we have not in the Income Tax Act the kind of amendments we were expecting fpr the encouragement of exports, I say that we are entitled to hear from the Minister of Finance some reference to this matter.
Then I think there is across the country great concern about the publicity that has been given to the administration of the Department of National Revenue in relation to assessing the proper deductions for church gifts. As recently as last week, on July 6, it was indicated in he Devoir-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. There is in this bill nothing to which that subject is related. That surely is a matter for the estimates of the Department of National Revenue, if my hon. friend wishes to raise it. This bill has nothing to do with the Department of National Revenue. It is simply a bill to amend the Income Tax Act.

As Your Honour knows, when we receive an amending bill we are certainly entitled to consider those suggested amendments that are in the bill, but surely we are also permitted to comment upon the things which should be in the bill but which are not in it. It is in this respect that I say what is being done administratively, without an amendment to the act, which might be changing practice under cabinet order in council or otherwise gives ground to this kind of press comment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member continuing his speech, or is he discussing the point of order now?
I was discussing the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member has something to add I will hear him.

That is my point of order; that this is very important in connection with the revenues which might be raised as a result of our income tax statute. I suggest to Your Honour that when we find significant comments across the country-I could quote from a great number of newspapers which have been asking about this subject within the past two or three weeks-this is a time for the House of Commons to ask the minister what will be realized in tax revenue under our income tax statute by reason of the regulations which are passed by order in council under the act, and by reason of the policy of those who collect income tax for us in the Department of National Revenue. If there is to be a significant change in the maximum allowance with respect to gifts which will be counted as charitable donations, I say this is the time when the minister should be asked about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say at once that there is nothing in this bill which touches on that subject at all. This is a bill containing certain amendments to certain clauses of the Income Tax Act. My respectful submission is that such subjects as the hon. member now proposes to discuss are altogether outside the realm of relevancy in this debate. The hon. member will have his opportunity to raise such questions on the estimates of the Department of National Revenue.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make an observation or two before you make your ruling on this important point. My hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River put the whole matter in a nutshell when he said that on an act to amend the Income Tax Act following the budget it is surely not to become the doctrine of the minister and certain hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches that we are not to be allowed to point out deficiencies, any kind of deficiencies, we think there are in the amendments that are being offered. The suggestion that the scope of our debate in this house should be limited to what hon. gentlemen sitting on the treasury benches think we are entitled to speak about and nothing else is preposterous.
I have in my hand, sir, something which I happened by sheer chance to have, and it is relevant to this very point. This is a report which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of March 22, 1957 of a speech made by the present Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition. It is headed "Parliament Puppet of Few Cabinet Ministers". The Minister of Finance, by saying we can only discuss what he in his wisdom thinks we should discuss and what he has chosen to put in this bill, is trying to make parliament a

Income Tax Act
puppet of one cabinet minister and to abridge our freedom of speech. It is just another example of that same kind of dictatorship-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate realizes, I suppose, that he is not addressing himself to the point of order at all.
Precisely.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has not discussed the question of relevancy. He has discussed the attitude of the minister-
I have a few words to say on the point of relevancy.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should like to hear the hon. member on that.

My hon. friend sought to say-and I was listening to him with care and attention-that certain administrative changes with regard to income tax appear to be in process without any legislative basis. He was contending that if such administrative changes were to be made there should be a legislative basis for them, and that this basis should be in the present bill. Surely nothing could be more relevant than that.

believe it has long been accepted in this house that at the resolution stage which in most cases precedes a bill such as this hon. members have the right to propose matters which in their opinion ought to be contained in the bill when it is brought down. I believe, also, that hitherto it has always been accepted that on second reading of a bill, the stage in which we are now engaged, members are permitted wide leeway to express their regret at the exclusion of matters which in their view ought to have been contained in the bill but which in fact are not contained in it.
As I understood the tenor of the comment of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, it was an expression of regret that measures which in his opinion ought to have been contained in the bill are not to be found in it. I agree that when we reach the committee stage we are usually tightly tied to discussion of what actually appears in the bill itself, but if hon. members will recall such occasions as the famous pipe line debate, and many other occasions, they will realize that while we were discussing the principles of the bill we were also permitted to express our regret that certain other matters were not included in the measure before the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I should like to say a word or two on this point of order. It is perfectly obvious what the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is trying to do. He is

trying to drag in something which has absolutely nothing to do with the bill now before the house. Now the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam tries to drag in the pipe line debate in support of the hon. member's contention that he is in order. I suggest this is going from the sublime to the ridiculous.
The house is now considering a particular bill, and if it were permissible for hon. members to raise any other points they pleased with regard to income tax, dealing with subjects not dealt with in the bill, there would be absolutely no limit to the scope of the debate. To allow a discussion of that kind would be to reduce the rules to a farce, and I submit to Your Honour that the statement made by the Minister of Finance in this regard is absolutely correct.
I do not know whether it is because at one time he was secretary to the late Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King or whether it is because at one time he was clerk to the privy council, but the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate considers himself to be a great authority on the House of Commons, on the rules and on everything else in public life in Canada. I suggest that today he is going much too far, and that he would be wiser to get back in his proper place and not make such a show as he has made of himself today and on previous occasions in the last few weeks.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On the point of order, it certainly would be reducing the rules to a farce if those rules were interpreted in the way in which the hon. gentleman has suggested they should be interpreted, namely in a way which would prevent the discussion, on an income tax bill, of those matters which have traditionally been the subject of discussion on the second reading of such a measure. I cannot understand why hon. gentlemen opposite should be trying once again to limit and prohibit discussion of subjects which are appropriate for discussion on a bill of this kind.

speakeroldname: Mr. M. J. A. Lambert (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I think the Leader of the Opposition and those supporting him would agree that if we were to follow their suggestion that the introduction of a bill containing, say, one clause dealing with the Income Tax Act would open the whole of the act to a general, wide ranging discussion, the house will be left in an impossible position. That has never been our practice. Certainly the rules of relevancy are being breached here, and I submit that only the items in this bill are capable of being discussed.
That is true in committee.
It is not true of second reading.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before dealing with this point might I just mention that there is a tendency, when discussing a point of order, for hon. members to discuss extraneous matters. Also, I should like to indicate that it is the duty of hon. members to raise points of order so that the rules may be applied. I do not think it is appropriate to *criticize hon. members for bringing forward points of order assisting the Chair to apply the rules.
In connection with the point of order which has been raised, I have been attempting to find some reference in May which indicates that on second reading amendments are admissible to a bill which introduce matters which are relevant to the bill. Reversing that principle, I think hon. members will agree that a discussion in relation to matters which ;annot be the subject of amendments would ae out of order.
The principle of the bill before us is to be found in the various clauses of the Income Tax Act which are proposed to be amended. It has been decided on several occasions that an amending bill does not open a discussion in respect to the full act to be amended, but only a discussion in respect to the sections of the act to be amended.
Hon. members may feel that they would like to discuss other problems, but I should like to remind them that during the debate on the budget, for instance, there was occasion for such a discussion in relation to subjects which were not touched upon. When a problem arises as to the administration or insufficiency of an act, a further opportunity for discussion is afforded when the estimates of the particular department concerned are before the house.
While I do not suggest one should use a knife to draw the line, I would say that in respect to matters of relevancy such as this -I am not enunciating anything new-I think the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is going somewhat outside the scope of the bill in discussing provisions which are not proposed to be amended, but which he would like to have amended. I refer hon. members to a decision by Mr. Speaker Macdonald on November 14, 1949, as reported in Journals of the House of Commons for that year at page 237, which reads in part as follows:
On the second reading of an amending hill- (honourable members will notice that this is an amending bill)-it is the principle of the amending bill, and not the principle of the act to be amended, which is the "business under consideration". The discussion must therefore relate exclusively to the principle of the amending bill.
The principle of an amending bill may not be found in a section of the act which is not
Income Tax Act
being amended. I also refer to a decision by Mr. Speaker Michener on December 13, 1957 during the consideration of a motion for second reading of Bill No. 232, to amend the Income Tax Act, as reported at page 2313 of Hansard for that year. It reads in part as follows:
This is an act to amend the Income Tax Act and it is relevant, as I understand the precedents, to discuss the sections of the Income Tax Act which are to be amended by this bill but not to review the act as a whole.
I therefore do not feel I need add anything further to indicate the general scope of the bill to hon. members, and I think the discussion should be limited to those subjects found in the bill proposing amendments to the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to address myself to your ruling, with all respect, in respect to the principle of the bill. I should like Your Honour to indicate to the house what principle can be found in the bill which is amending, helter skelter, a number of sections of the Income Tax Act.
I remind Your Honour that this amending bill was preceded by a resolution presented on budget night, and as a preliminary to the introdution of this resolution there is a statement which reads:
Resolved,-that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide among other things-
It has been traditional that among the other things we will find when the bill comes forward, as we did only two weeks ago, there are items not exclusively connected with the enunciations made in the resolution on budget night. I find it impossible in this amending bill to find anything to which Your Honour refers as the principle. While I realize Your Honour's purpose, sometimes in an amending bill we find there is a principle involved, but can Your Honour indicate to us now any principle involved in this amending bill other than the principle that the Income Tax Act has to be amended once a year? When the act is being amended surely it is proper for us to comment upon those things which are not referred to and not being amended, particularly when there is no striking principle among the multiplicity of amendments that appear in the bill amending a statute which involves nearly 100 sections?

Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question. Supposing we had a bill with only one clause amending only one section of the Income Tax Act. Does the hon. member suggest that would entitle hon. members to range over the whole act asking questions about

Income Tax Act
and suggesting recommendations to every section? That seems to be what he is arguing.

Mr. Speaker, I have been asked to answer a specific question by the hon. member for Greenwood. Perhaps he might define the principle contained in this amending bill. I suggest that we have never, to my knowledge at any rate, under the universal requirement of amending the Income Tax Act and making a great number of changes, many of which are not simply in respect to tax rates but relate to administration and interpretation of law with respect to the Income Tax Act, been prevented from discussing such matters. I suggest the hon. member's question is irrelevant because he knows, as a result of his experience during all the time he has been here, that there never has been an amendment to the Income Tax Act after a budget speech which has been confined to one section or could be regarded as involving one obvious principle. I suggest the bill presently before us involves a conglomeration of amendments. If the hon. member can tell me what the principle is which is involved, I should like him to do so.
For the reasons I have given I submit that omissions should be referred to. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Revenue has intervened. I am glad to see that he is in the house, because he will have an opportunity to speak on second reading today in the absence of the minister, who we all regret is away due to illness. I think it is very important that when we are considering ways and means of amending the Income Tax Act, which affects our ultimate revenue, opinions as to how revenue should be raised should be considered in fairness to us all. When a statement is made indicating that the administration is proposing something new, which I think is consequential, and when it is reported in the press that income tax inspectors have set a maximum of $300-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the point of order, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is now going to make the speech he commenced to make, on which you made a ruling. I suggest he is now ignoring your ruling; that he has attempted to have you change your mind and has now reverted to his main argument. I submit that upon your ruling the point of order was dealt with, and that the hon. member has no right whatsoever to go ahead now dealing with this subject. Surely when Your Honour makes a ruling that should be final.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member should not be allowed to continue arguing about the point of order after your decision has been made.

Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has now raised a new point of order. It is interesting to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs say that he remembers what happened in 1956, when his party was in opposition, and that the Speaker's decision should be final. That is a view I have always held, but it is not the view that hon. gentlemen opposite have held.
On the point that my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River made as to the principle of the bill, which was the point Your Honour was considering in the statement Your Honour made for the guidance of the house- and I did not understand Your Honour made a ruling; Your Honour simply indicated the lines on which he thought the debate ought to proceed-it seems to me that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River made a conclusive case that the only principle in this bill, and the only possible principle one could find anywhere, is that the Income Tax Act is not perfect as it is now and ought to be amended in a number of particulars which are set out in 36 pages. Surely the opposition, if it is to have any rights, has the right to say on the principle that these are not the right amendments, that there are other amendments which are more desirable than these. Otherwise, sir, what is debate? If we have simply to niggle about the clauses of the bill on second reading, why do we not just go into committee and have no second reading? Surely the purpose of second reading is to debate whether the bill itself is adequate. My hon. friend is seeking to show that in one particular respect this bill is inadequate, and shockingly inadequate; and the Minister of Finance, as is his habit in this house, is seeking to gag him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Is the hon. member speaking on the point of order?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I sat here very quietly but I could not resist rising and saying something in support of the previous speaker. I do not think in fairness the minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs should try to narrow the discussion on second reading of the bill at this time, which is quite out of keeping with the practices of the past.
I agree with what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said with respect to the principle. You, sir, made reference to the principle of the bill, but there is no specific principle. This bill amends the Income Tax Act. I want to bring to your attention the fact that surely we must have the opportunity, in dealing with this legislation, to suggest that there are deficiencies here and there.

For instance, clause 9 provides certain exemptions for a spouse and dependents. Surely we have the right to say that aunties should be included as well. Certain business expenses are permitted to be deducted. I should like to see the travelling expenses of certain employees included. Surely we have the right to make suggestions as to further additions and amendments, and are not restricted to saying "amen" to each clause as it comes before the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Kootenay West for his assistance. I think he has said something that is true, and I shall come back to this later, but 1 should like to deal first with the points raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River who asked what is the principle of an amending bill. Well, there may be as many principles in an amending bill as there are clauses amended or new clauses inserted in the act. For clarification of the point I would venture to say that it is not necessary to enumerate them all. For instance, there is a clause which would allow a deduction on account of expenditures for scientific research up to 5 per cent of the taxable income. That is a principle. There may be another one in the amendments which provides a new manner of taxation of shareholders of personal corporations.
In connection with these matters, the hon. member for Kootenay West has said that the house does not have to say "amen" to each clause. For example, in dealing with clause 25, if he said that we should allow up to 10 per cent instead of 5 per cent for scientific research, then he would be in order because he would be dealing with something which is in the act. But the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River wanted to discuss clauses which are not amended, and say he is disappointed because the amending legislation may cover more subjects than the resolution did.
The subject matter before the house is certainly this bill and nothing else. There will be other occasions to discuss other matters. Only on Saturday I said the main difficulty is that hon. members do not want to discuss the problems at hand but always want to discuss something other than the business before the house. I think I have made myself clear, and I should be understood by all hon. members.
Mr. Speaker, I think that is rather a narrow decision. However, I will confine myself to it at the moment. I simply make the observation that this certainly was not the practice in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It certainly was the past practice.

speechtext: Order. The hon. member should not discuss a decision of the Chair. Since he has brought up the point may I remind him that I quoted a decision of Mr. Speaker Macdonald.
Not on income tax bills.
Order.
Are you questioning it?

Yes. I will say that here is a Minister of Finance who has said that he had not, when he was on this side of the house, adopted the style of debate that I have adopted. I say that is wrong. I recall very clearly when on an income tax bill he protested very vigorously that it did not include the exemption from sales tax of boots and shoes for children; that the exemption for married people should be $3,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I hope the hon. member will come back to the bill. The point of order has been dealt with.

Mr. Speaker, I continue to say that certain other matters should be included. Before the minister concludes the debate on second reading we should hear from him about those matters.
In his budget speech the minister referred to a tightening up of certain exemptions, and I approve of this course. The reference was to the tightening up of certain exemptions that may have been claimed for business expenses and so on. Inasmuch as the minister dealt with these things in his budget speech, I would hope we might hear from him about them, because there is nothing in this bill relating to them. This is administrative.
The crown is employing legal agents to prosecute people for tax evasions, and this is vital to every clause of the bill. We have to know the type of enforcement that will be applied to make sure that the law that is passed by us here is going to be enforced in a certain manner. In connection with tax evasion in an important case-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member cannot discuss the problem of tax evasion unless the amendments bring new problems in this respect. I do not know whether I am correct, but it seems to me that the hon. member is referring again to the problem which brought on the point of order and the decision of the Chair.

No, Mr. Speaker, I was not referring to the previous item. I am referring to an administrative application and enforcement of tax laws which will relate to every clause in this bill. Some of these clauses

Income Tax Act
impose new taxation. We all know in connection with these matters that in a small percentage of the cases there is tax evasion. We want to know whether there is going to be something new in the matter of investigation, prosecution and other relationships connected with all the clauses of this bill which impose new taxation. A representative of the crown in a recent prosecution said it is very likely that prosecution by indictment, which carries with it a mandatory jail term on conviction, will be the procedure in the future in cases of tax evasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker-
I think we are entitled to know whether that is going to be so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -there is nothing in this bill that relates to that subject, and the hon. member is talking about something that was said in the budget. Everything that was said in the budget does not become relevant to this particular bill. We have already disposed of three bills that arose out of the budget. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Because you talk so much.

I want to discuss a theory to which I referred in a speech I made last December, and which has to do with a profit sharing plan. The profit sharing plan has been-

speechtext: Order. Could the hon. member indicate to which section of the bill he is referring, or how he relates his remarks to the bill before us?

Mr. Speaker, reference is made in paragraph (a) of section 1 of this bill to a deferred profit sharing plan. Besides, it is referred to all through the bill. Well, I want to establish the relationship which exists between the profit sharing plan and the consequent tax. So, I believe I am not out of order in dealing with this.
In my opinion, a deferred profit sharing plan is a concrete form of a middle course theory between egotistical materialism, which is generally condemned, and exaggerated unionism, which is often the cause of trouble in our economy. In fact, such a middle course for employers and employees would help solve many of the problems we have to face nowadays.
It is a co-operative formula which enters in the solution of many a conflict. It ensures the welfare and security of the worker, on the one hand, and increases industrial production and improves the economy in general, on the other.
We are looking for new theories which deserve consideration, and very often the ones we adopt are ill-suited to our needs. For instance, various parties preach economic theories. Last week, we heard' the Social Credit party state its own theory, the implementation of which would be just as difficult, in my opinion, as it would be for me to go to the moon on a bicycle.
There is also the theory of the party which sits on our right, the C.C.F. party, the Socialist party, the New party-the name under which it hides itself is of no importance-which advocates a socialist theory not far from that of Marx.
How can this deferred profit sharing plan apply? As I have already indicated, it is not, of course, the government's responsibility to impose this plan to Canada's economy.

Before we enter into any discussion on the specific content of the clause I think I will take advantage of what I described as the Howard Green rule, which was given an odour of sanctity by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs when he sat on this side of the house and which provided for a certain amount of general discussion on the first clause of a bill. You, sir, may not have been following what was going on this morning. This is a very peculiar bill. We have been told by a number of

Income Tax Act
persons it is a bill without a principle and, apparently, without much purpose.
Nevertheless it does contain provisions that are going to change the Income Tax Act, and it some of these changes are carried through they will have varying effects upon the Canadian people. This is provided the government does not change its mind, and perhaps in a few minutes the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River will give us the statistics to indicate how many times they have changed their mind about this bill since budget night. If the government do not change their minds many more times, when their majority has dealt with these changes in the income tax they will have varying effects upon the Canadian people. We will, as we always do, consider each of these clauses strictly on its merits and the effect each of them will have on the Canadian people.
Notwithstanding the minister's great desire for a holiday, which the government leader expressed on Friday evening by saying the minister would be content to stop at second reading of this bill; notwithstanding that fact, the minister chose to take up the time of the house by having a recorded vote on second reading of the bill, we, of course, could do nothing else but vote against this bill, because we consider it hopelessly inadequate in ways we were not allowed to explain to deal with the present serious economic condition in this country. I do not want to attempt to revive the debate on second reading, but I want to point out that we regard this as a very puny expression of the great expansion that was heralded in this country on June 14 and is really ending in a whimper.

As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has said, there is nothing very devastating in the amendments here Which involve the average taxpayer of Canada. When we are looking at clause 1, perhaps the minister could explain the benefits that accrue under the deferred profit sharing plans. I think the minister would want to go beyond the explanation he made on June 20, and I invite him to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the main provisions of this bill concerning deferred profit sharing plans are to be found in clause 27. Clause 1 of the bill simply is consequential upon the introduction of a new class of profit sharing plans provided for by clause 27, which would bring within the provisions of section 5 of the act any contributions made on account of a profit sharing plan.

The minister will agree that he has had some hesitation in introducing

a bill into this House of Commons with respect to deferred profit sharing plans, because he introduced such a bill during the 1960 session and allowed it to lapse. I ask him to indicate to the committee the result of negotiations or discussions that might have taken place during this period. I hope he will do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we received quite generous consideration from those to whom we appealed for their views with regard to amendments to the Income Tax Act in relation to such plans. It is in the light of the representations which we received in response to that appeal, following the draft bill which was introduced in the 1960 session, that our study of the matter has gone further and that, in accordance with the resolution which the house approved, Bill No. C-120 now contains extensive provisions in relation to deferred profit sharing plans.
The provisions of this bill, of course, are not the same as those of the draft bill of the 1960 session. The provisions of this bill have been prepared in the light of the representations that have been made to us. We think it is a very good and workable scheme that has been put forward. Whereas previously the only provision the act made was in relation to other classes of profit sharing, now we have provision made for the deferred profit sharing plan. Under this measure the contribution of the employer on behalf of the employees to such a plan is given exemption in relation to the employer's income. The benefit that will be payable to the employee on retirement-and this is the purpose of the deferment that is contemplated in the deferred profit sharing plan-will be taxable like any other income at that time. As I pointed out in the budget speech, there are special provisions in cases where the employee in such a case has chosen to take up residence outside of Canada. This we consider to be a well balanced scheme to give encouragement to deferred profit sharing plans. We think there is a great deal of social benefit in such plans and that the Income Tax Act should be so revised now as to encourage employers to establish such plans so their employees may benefit substantially at the time of retirement.

I have no over-all quarrel with the minister's objectives, but I remind the committee that last year he even introduced a bill which was supposed to take account of the opportunity for deferred profit sharing plan operations within a corporation as between employees and employers. The minister wanted a year of reconsideration for his officials. In this bill I find nothing that indicates to me that the year has brought any

useful information. I think we in the opposition, small as we are in numbers, are entitled to the complete consensus of the advice that has been given to the Department of Finance on that bill introduced by the minister a year ago. What were the objections to amendments of statutes that are suggested here? To what extent has the government changed its mind since it introduced its pilot bill a year ago in 1960? I think these things should be discussed with respect to the plan for deferred profit sharing of employees and the corporations concerned in Bill C-84 compared with the plan that is involved in clause 1 of this amending bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We had a score or more of representations from different sources. The professional groups made their representations. I have listened to the minister, Mr. Chairman, but I do not think he has indicated to all of us the differences between the opinions he had as expressed in the bill introduced by him last year and any action that is required by us in parliament a year later on this bill amending the Income Tax Act. I ask the minister to review for us what has taken place between March, 1960 and the present time. We would normally expect a budget, of course, in March 1961. We did not get it. I ask him to tell us what the changes have been as a result of the advice he received a year ago.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: On subsection 2 I should like some information. I must admit that I am not a lawyer, and I am asking the minister for information. The amendment provides, in underlined words, that travelling and living allowances need not be included in income. Would that mean that a gentleman travelling from either Ottawa or Montreal to Quebec for lobbying and getting compensation for it would not have to include in any amount which he might receive, as a total amount his travelling and living expenses while he was lobbying in Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This clause, as I am sure the hon. member will realize on examination, relates to something altogether different. It relates to the expense allowance provided for any person whose services are engaged pursuant to the Inquiries Act. This clause is introduced for the purpose of clarification. It provides that per diem allowances paid to members of royal commissions to cover travelling or living expenses need not be included in income. These allowances have not been regarded as taxable income in the past, but in view of the fact that some doubt has arisen because of the language of the present act it is deemed advisable to ask parliament to clarify the law.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: As I said before, I am not a lawyer. The minister will admit that my question was a fair one. I think it is only fair that we should know exactly what we are supporting.

In connection with subclause 2 of clause 1, I take it the minister is saying that the administration has up to now observed the law in a way which is in accordance with what was stated to the hon. member for Cochrane. The minister is saying there is no change in the law as far as this wording is concerned. I take it this provision means that we are rectifying or rationalizing what we have been doing for some time. Is that possible? We have had a large number of people appointed to commissions under the Inquiries Act in recent times. This government cannot make up its mind itself. The process involves the appointment of royal commissions all the time, and these are just delaying tactics before a decision is reached.
That is what is involved here. These people who are appointed by the government to royal commissions will receive certain concessions under this income tax bill. I do not object

to that. I think we need inquiries of this kind at times. However, I want to ask the minister specifically whether this implies anything different from what was allowed to those who sat on commissions appointed by this government in the last two or three years. Are commissioners now to receive benefits additional to those which were received formerly by reason of this subsection and, if so, why? Who is going to be appointed under the Inquiries Act to make for this government decisions which the government should make for itself? Will the minister give us a record of the per diem allowances which have been provided to those acting on royal commissions set up by this government under the Inquiries Act? Will he give us, per person and per inquiry, figures showing what will be involved if we pass this clause concerning travelling and living allowances which may be deducted from income for taxation purposes?
I believe this country owes a great debt to people who are ready to take the time to look at some of the economic, social and other problems which we face today, when invited by their government so to do, but we must regard this matter carefully. Twenty years ago we used to think that somebody of my profession, a lawyer, had no particular advantage if he was appointed a member of a commission under the Inquiries Act to perform services for which he received a per diem rate of pay. He was sneered at because he received a per diem rate of pay. I want to make sure we are doing nothing here which will be in any way a departure from a new attitude which is growing up, namely that people who are asked by their government to serve on inquiries are not likely to be profiteers. I hope we have reached the point where nobody who is required by his government to give his time to the tremendously important concerns which parliament may refer to a commission under the Inquiries Act may be challenged and told he has served there to his advantage in dollars and cents. I hope this amendment to the bill does not provide that opportunity.
As a young man, years ago, I had an idea that it was advantageous to serve in the depression of the thirties in one capacity or another for $100 a day. As I have matured I have grown to understand that this country can enlist and command the services of the most important people in this country if we make sure that we do so on the basis of personal sacrifice and national advantage. I question clause 3 because I do not want political heelers any longer to become connected with these national inquiries and commissions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the full provisions in relation to deferred profit sharing plans are in clause 27, which we will be considering shortly. This clause simply has the effect of bringing into taxable income the benefits received by a taxpayer under the deferred profit sharing plan. This means that in the ordinary course, when he retires, the benefits he receives become income and consequently taxable.
Income Tax Act
Mr. Chairman, I believe it was in March 1960 when the minister introduced the budget he said he intended to introduce a special bill in respect of deferred profit sharing plans.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
As I indicated
earlier, when we are dealing with clause 27 we will have the provisions before us and we can see what are the differences between the provisions of this bill and those put forward in the draft bill of 1960. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Before clause 2 carries, I should like to say a few words. There are many references in this bill to profit sharing programs. I think the minister should give us an indication at this time what he is going to do with these accumulations which, if they related to pensions, would be called vestings. Many companies declare a certain amount of money available for profit sharing, and this may take two or three forms. Some companies put it in the form of shares in the company, other companies in the form of cash. In some companies, the money to which the employee is entitled is paid to him somewhat along the same lines as compulsory savings, that is paid to him on retirement.

Income Tax Act
I believe the minister should give us an indication of his thinking in relation to the charge that is made by the department when these funds are in the form of shares or accumulated savings for retirement. One of the questions that will be asked, of course, is what happens when the man is fired? Is his share in that year, if it is near the end of the year, given to someone else? What protection is to be given in order to dispel fear that will be in the minds of many Canadians who are directly interested in the welfare of the workers through union activity? There seems to be some reference to the elimination of the anti-union aspect in this which indicates that companies, rather than giving increases in wages will introduce profit sharing plans.
I think before we pass the first clause that refers to these plans, we should know what the minister's thinking is in regard to this aspect which would be mainly involved in vesting if we were dealing with pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This has nothing to do with pensions or the vesting of pensions. That is a different subject altogether. This clause refers to deferred profit sharing plans, and when we come to clause 27 we will have the provisions before us.

I think without a doubt the minister will go down in Canadian parliamentary history as the outstanding man in the field for not answering questions by raising points of order and having other members ruled out of order when they attempt to obtain legitimate answers to their questions. The hon. member for Timiskaming pointed out, most adequately, that this was the first of many amendments contained in this bill. Before we signify our approval to even the very first item, we should know what the intentions of this government are with regard to protecting the interests of these workers in Canada who will agree, in preference to ordinary pension agreements as we know them, to participate in profit sharing arrangements.
As the hon. member pointed out, in the final analysis, as to its extent, this is always at the discretion of management at the end of the year. If the company have made a net profit of $100 million, they may decide to share $10 million of it with their employees or they may desire to share only $1 million with their employees. We are now beginning to grant concessions to the companies and these are not concessions being granted to the workers. Let us be very clear about this matter. This is the beginning of granting to companies the right to declare such profit sharing arrangements as part of their regular wage bill or as a substitution, if you like,
IMr. Peters.]
of a regular wage bill which ordinarily would be exempt under the terms of the Income Tax Act. Before we are prepared to begin granting this right to companies, and it involves millions of dollars in the case of a goodly number of companies I might name, I believe we are entitled to ask the government what are its intentions under this act with regard to protecting the rights of the workers. Far too many workers have had most regrettable experience when it came to a lack of vesting rights as far as their pensions were concerned and companies have repeatedly taken advantage-legally it is right, but morally most wrong-under the Income Tax Act. I feel that the minister owes us an explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This, of course, is a first class example of the confusion that arises when we do not deal with the clauses of the bill seriatim in accordance with the rules. The clauses of the bill in relation to deferred profit sharing plans and the tax treatment of those plans and all questions associated with them are to be found in clause 27 of the bill. When we reach that clause there will be an opportunity for an orderly discussion. All that this clause does is to say that any benefits received under such a plan are taxable income and there is every reason why they should be so. To pass this clause does not preclude discussion.

On that very point, Mr. Chairman, may I say that the minister has just made it very clear that any benefit received under such a plan is taxable income. What I should like to know is this. Any benefit under such a plan accrues only to the company in that the companies now will be, as he has indicated, in subsequent sections granted very great concessions. I should like to know what concessions are provided in this bill for the protection of the legitimate interests of the workers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The answer to that is in clause 27 when we reach it.
The minister said something which caught my interest. He said this was simply a provision that these benefits should be taxable income. Have they not been taxable income hitherto?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. There has not been provision in the act up until the present time for a deferred profit sharing plan. Where there are profit sharing plans under which profits are shared at the time, then obviously they become taxable income in the hands of the employee recipient. We are now introducing provisions which will be found later in the bill and which contemplate

a new kind of plan, a deferred profit sharing plan, whereby the employee does not take out the profits at the time they are declared; instead they go into a fund and they will be accumulated there. He is not to be taxed on them while they are accumulating, even though payments are made into the fund on his behalf by his employer. There is a deferment of tax, because there is a deferment of enjoyment under the plan, until he takes out the proceeds. When the time comes under the terms of the plan to take them out, then of course they become taxable income just as they are now. Any profit sharing benefit now is taxable income.

Would that not be the
case under the present law even if this provision were not made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. That is what I am speaking of now. In relation to any benefit that is now drawn, the employee is taxable in respect thereof as taxable income. The purpose of the deferred profit sharing plan is to relieve him of any tax in respect of contributions made into the deferred profit sharing plan by his employer on his behalf. He is not going to be taxed on those while they are in the plan and accumulating there. When he takes them out on retirement, then under this clause they will be taxable.

I am not sure that I have this thing quite straight and I will try to put the point as simply as I can in order to see whether I have it straight. Is it the case now-if I may have the minister's attention-that even though they are paying into a deferred plan, they are taxed now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. That is the whole point.
Oh, I see. That is what I was seeking to get at. What this does is to treat them in the same way as contributions to a pension fund are treated-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There will be a deferment in respect of them.

Perhaps it would be a little bit easier if the minister would let me finish my sentences. I am really not seeking to make difficulties for him; I am seeking quite the reverse. What I am saying is this. As I see it now-and it is beginning to be quite clear-
It is beginning to dawn.

Yes; that is quite right. It is beginning to dawn. I do not apologize for that for unlike the minister I am not an expert on these matters. As I understand it now, if an employee receives a benefit under a profit sharing plan, even though he does not
Income Tax Act
get it in cash but it goes into a deferment which he will receive at some future date, he has to pay income tax on it in this tax year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Just as at one time I believe it was true that even though you put money aside in a pension fund, before a change was made some years ago in the income tax it was taxed. This is just treating profit sharing in the same way as contributions to pension funds are now treated with approved pension plans.
If it is deferred.
Pensions, of course, would be deferred. That is the situation if this is deferred, as the pensions are.

speechtext: Yes. Anybody who draws a present benefit under such a plan will continue to be taxable, in other words, if there is a profit sharing plan effective now. That is quite right; that is sensible.

I have read and reread the remarks of the minister on June 20 when he in effect took off the ceiling on the expenses of a taxpayer for medical purposes. He certainly aroused our sympathy by some of the illustrations he mentioned on June 20. However, I recall that this was resisted in the past by those who had some regard for the revenue of the crown, not on the grounds of inhumanity at all, but on the grounds that it might give a special privilege to people who might misuse this right of tax deduction if there were not some regulations. I am getting a little aged myself. Can I be assured that I would not be permitted to go down to Florida with a nurse, in the interests of my health, and that after certification the expenses of the

Income Tax Act
beautiful nurse and, of course, the doctor's expenses that might be attributed to my requirements would not qualify under this clause that removes the ceiling? I think that was the attitude in the past.
I have regard for the fact that the purchasing power of the dollar has decreased considerably in recent years. The wages of those whom we employ and need for our medical health continue to go up. In the past our reason for having a ceiling here was to make it impossible for the ultra-rich to get a special benefit in so far as tax deduction was concerned by, as I say, going to health homes that were not open to the ordinary person but were open to the wealthy taxpayer where he could go with all the accoutrements that might be called specialized services. speechtext: There is no change in the definition of what are admissible medical expenses. The clause simply removes the ceiling. As I suggested in the budget speech, one man as a result of misfortune may incur as large medical expenses in one year as another man may incur in a lifetime. Last year we invited the house to increase the permissible ceilings and the house responded. I think I may say that there was quite a measure of warm approbation of the proposal voiced in all parts of the house. This year we are asking the house to go a step further and remove that ceiling and, I think, to do so in the interests of fairness for all taxpayers who may have this misfortune.

I have the utmost sympathy for all taxpayers who have a very heavy burden of expense in connection with ill health, accident or otherwise. I just want to make sure that we are not creating here an opportunity for inequality in the tax advantage that is possible under our law in respect of this provision. I recall that in the past I supported a ceiling on the maximum amount of deduction that would be possible. I would support today a spreading or averaging of legitimate, unavoidable and unfortunate medical expenses in one year over perhaps three or four years.

I simply raise the question here whether this provision does not give people in a very high income bracket an opportunity deliberately denied them in the past whereby such people were not able to deduct as a medical expense the cost of a qualified nurse or somebody else to push around a sick person in a wheel chair in Florida. I raised this matter in past years simply on the ground of fairness in our income tax structure. I quite agree with what the minister said on June 20 with respect to the catastrophic results in the case of a taxpayer involved in an automobile accident, let us say, who has expenses going away beyond the maximum deduction that has been allowed up to now. Having regard to our progressive tax rates I simply raise the question of whether or not in fairness the amendment would not have been better if we had allowed, in the case of an excessive amount of medical expenses, a carryover from one year to the next so that a taxpayer having an excessive amount of medical expenses in
1961	could average them over the years 1961,
1962	and 1963. I am solely concerned with the facts of life here. This is a matter to which I paid a great deal of attention when I was on the other side and I was persuaded that such a move was not desirable because the complete removal of the ceiling on deductions with regard to medical expenses could result in unfairness between the rich and the poor.

I have one question on clause 9, subclause 1. The amendment adds the underlined words "laryngeal speaking aid" so that the cost of such a speaking aid can be included in medical expenses. Can the minister inform the committee whether there are other types of speaking aids than laryngeal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This refers to speaking aids for those who have suffered cancer of the throat.
It does not provide for other types of speaking aids?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I am not aware of other kinds that enable individuals to speak. This speaking aid is one that is attached to the larynx in some way to enable someone who otherwise would not have the power to speak to be heard and understood when the apparatus is turned on.
Can we take it that it means any speaking aid that is required to aid a person to speak?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If it is a laryngeal aid, yes. It would not apply to a microphone or horn that somebody used to make himself heard in the great outdoors. It is one that is

related to the larynx in the sense that otherwise the larynx is not functioning in an audible way. The kind of speaking aid we are thinking of here is well known and it has brought back the power of speech to many who have suffered loss of speech through cancer of the throat.
I asked the question because there are other names used for different types of speaking aids and I wondered whether they were included.

Income Tax Act
I direct myself at the moment exclusively to the new amendment. Does it result from any representation from any other government such as that of the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.
I look at the explanatory notes-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I might say that this did emerge out of discussions with representatives of the tax foundation last week.

I go to the end of subclause (d) and I refer to the words:
.. . unless it can be established, by subsequent events or otherwise, that the payment was made as part of a series of annual or other periodic payments payable throughout the lifetime of the payee.
I direct my inquiry to those words although there is a much longer part of the new section 31A preceding them. Does that mean that in the opinion of the administration it must be almost on the basis of a perpetual income, a lifetime basis, if a person receives a benefit of this type for performance of a service in Canada and then resides elsewhere?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This provision
draws a line of distinction between lump sum payments and pension payments. This clause 11 of the bill, Mr. Chairman, deals with lump sum payments to former employees. It is designed to close a loophole.

I think the minister is endeavouring to assure that a longtime resident of Canada who has earned his income in Canada is not going to get from his employer, on conclusion of his employment, a substantial lump sum and then vanish to another country. I am referring to a capital sum, a lump sum.
I am concerned with the qualifications in the last part of this clause which refer, as I described a moment ago, to taxable lump sum payments when he leaves the country, and that is all that we can regard as his reward. I am concerned about the periodic payments. Do they have to be regular or are they only periodic to qualify under the provisions of this clause? In other words, is it going to be necessary, to avoid this impost, in the case of a person who has earned an entitlement from his company to a lump sum payment or some form of retirement award, that that reward be paid regularly up until the time of the death of the employee or does the word "periodic" have reference to a series of annual or other payments, perhaps for two or three years and

Income Tax Act
then we forget all about it? What has the administration in mind in introducing this protection? I am in sympathy with what the minister is trying to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member will look at lines 44 and 45, I think he will see the answer to his question. There is reference there to a series of annual or other periodic payments payable throughout the lifetime of the payee.

I saw that, and I just wanted confirmation of the fact that the reward payable after retirement to someone in Canada, before leaving Canada, would not be an undue amount, but it would be related more or less to an annuity. Would it be related more or less to an averaging out through his lifetime of a benefit, as is the case in connection with a pension fund? Why does the act not state that?
Perhaps I have not stated it too clearly. Why is it not clear here that it must be what I, in my ignorance, would call a pension or annuity rather than periodic payments payable throughout the lifetime of the payee? I raise this question with the minister. Would it be possible for a senior executive of an important corporation to receive, at the termination of his employment, a very large lump sum payment, with the other part of the recognition of his lifetime service still payable in annual or periodic but nominal payments throughout his lifetime? The language disturbs me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am doing my best to follow the hon. member, but I am having some difficulty. This language, a series of annual or other periodic payments payable throughout the lifetime of the payee, clearly means a pension for life. It may be payable in annual instalments or it may be payable in quarterly amounts or in some cases in monthly amounts. These are periodic payments and they are payable throughout the lifetime of the payee.

In other words, I would imagine it was the intention of the draftsman that if there was a capital value, let us say, of $50,000 of a retirement benefit it would not be possible in the contemplation of the department for the retiring employee who left Canada to receive $40,000 in cash and then receive an additional $10,000 in cash on the basis of annual or other periodic payments payable throughout the lifetime of the payee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the case put by my hon. friend, 1 think there is no doubt that the lump sum would be taxable, but

the pension that is payable on a true life basis, of course, would escape taxation.
