speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 13-Deduction from tax when resident, etc. in province.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I told the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that on clause 13 I would answer the question he asked when he was here and explained that he would not be able to be here when this clause would be reached. As the note indicates, this clause is to provide for a reduction of the personal income tax for the years 1962 to 1966 inclusive in accordance with new fiscal arrangements with the provinces commencing April 1, 1962.
The present Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act will expire or its operation will not extend beyond those payments provided for at the end of this present fiscal

year. Clause 13 is designed to lay the groundwork for certain reductions that will be provided under the federal income tax. The purpose will be to enable the provinces which desire to enter this tax field to occupy it to whatever extent they wish to occupy it. When we reach item No. 9 on the order paper I shall have something to say about the proposal made there by the federal government for the benefit of the provinces in relation to collecting provincial personal income tax and corporation tax. However, the purpose of this clause is to provide-and we have to do it this year in order to make it clearly applicable to next year and so that the provinces may make their plans this year accordingly-for the deduction from the basic federal tax. This could be done by way of an amendment each year in advance. We could have an amendment this year providing in 1962 a deduction of 16 per cent. We could have an amendment passed next year to provide that with respect to the year 1963 there would be a 17 per cent deduction and so on throughout the five year period. But it was in keeping with the wishes of the provinces that they should know clearly in advance by federal statutory enactment what the percentages would be, and so we are asking parliament to make this provision for the rising percentage of deductions from the federal income tax in favour of the provinces year by year for the next five years.

I do not intend to embark upon a debate upon item No. 9 on the order paper at this time. I do not think that procedure would be appropriate. However, we cannot possibly let this clause go by without pointing out what it is really seeking to do. If I sought for one word by means of which to describe this clause, I would call it the repudiation clause. We all remember that at the federal-provincial conference, not the last meeting but the one previous to the last one, the Prime Minister spoke and gave an unqualified undertaking that the principle of equalization would be maintained. This clause is a clear repudiation of the principle of equalization.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at all.

If the minister wishes to provoke a lengthier discussion, he can go ahead. However, I intend to say what I wish to say about this matter regardless of interruptions.
The principle of equalization is the principle that the revenues of the provinces from the three direct taxes shall be brought up to the level of the two top provinces-that is to say the two provinces with the highest per capita return from the income tax-in
Income Tax Act
respect of the rate that is allowed to the provinces as an abatement or a reduction from the federal rate. That is not expressed as felicitously as it is expressed in the statutes but I think the meaning is very clear.
The effect of what is being done here will be that those provinces which have the highest per capita income, particularly Ontario and British Columbia and really in fact only Ontario, will get a larger and larger share and the national treasury a smaller and smaller share of the total income tax collected in this country. That is what is going to happen. The principle of equalization is not totally abandoned. However, the principle of equalization is not being carried on in the way in which the Prime Minister in quite unqualified language to the premiers said it would be carried on.
When the minister said that this was to carry on the new arrangement with the provinces, that is certainly stretching the word "arrangement" far beyond any definition that the minister could find in any dictionary. An arrangement suggests at any rate some understanding between the parties. Anybody who has read what the premier of Manitoba, a supporter of this government, has had to say about this subject, to say nothing of some of the things that are said by the premier of Saskatchewan and some of the other premiers including the premier of New Brunswick will have no doubt that there was no arrangement whatsoever. There was a "diktat" which was called a suggestion. But these soft words do not change the real nature of things. The provinces were told this: "You can go and collect your own taxes. If you fix them on our scheme without any deviation, and if your act is a direct copy of the federal act, we will collect the taxes for you, but you have got to impose them yourself and that is final. If you make any variation whatsoever in your scheme, then you collect them yourself too."
Of course there were two purposes in doing this. The hon. gentlemen who now occupy the treasury benches, and particularly the leader of the government, had promised Mr. Frost $100 million, and they could not find $100 million to give him by the front door. This is an attempt to give him an instalment of it by the back door without giving anything comparable to the other provinces. That is what it is. It is making a large area, which will ultimately be 20 per cent in the case of the present income tax available to Ontario and also, it is true, available to Newfoundland, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and New Brunswick as well but without any equalization to those provinces. Ontario will get indeed as a benefit into its treasury more than the amount under equalization, as it

Income Tax Act
does now, of course, because equalization is based on two provinces, not one. But even in Ontario it is a great deal less than Mr. Frost was promised in those happy days of long ago in 1957.
Everybody was let down.

But Mr. Frost has been discounted only by 50 per cent or 60 per cent. Some of the other provinces are being discounted by 70 per cent or 80 per cent or more of what was promised in those days. However, as I say, I am not going to enter into an extended debate at this stage. There is another stage when that can be done. However, I just wanted to be sure that nobody in the committee was under any illusion about what this is. Of course, it is going to look good. The federal tax is going to go down; although the provincial tax will go up at least as much. But then they will be able to say, "Look at what we did for you". Then they will say "that wretched fellow out there in Alberta" or in Saskatchewan, perhaps they will not say "wretched fellow" in Manitoba but they will say "unfortunate fellow". Of course, the person whose body is really laid on the altar by this proposal is the premier of Manitoba. I imagine that every time the premier of Manitoba thinks of that slogan he used, namely "What Dief did, Duff will do" he undoubtedly wishes he had never said it because what Dief has done to Duff, Duff will never be able to undo. And this is where it is being done-right here in this repudiation clause of this bill to amend the Income Tax Act. Everybody in Manitoba knows it. Of course, it is being glossed over by various other provisions which would be beyond the scope of this bill, and I am not going to cause you any pain, Mr. Chairman, by dealing with those other things. The plain fact is that no concession is being made to anybody by this, not even Ontario. It is true that Ontario will receive a larger share of the personal income tax than the province is getting now. That is true. The share will be a little larger. But it will be nothing like what was held out with great hope and without requiring any action of the Ontario legislature four years ago.
Perhaps I was rash. Perhaps I should not have said that one word would describe this clause. This clause can be described as the repudiation and disillusion clause. It means disillusionment for Mr. Frost and deeper disillusionment for the premier of every other province in this country. Everyone knows that I am not normally a tremendous admirer of the premier of Saskatchewan but he has a capacity in this particular field, which he

understands very well, to express things exactly, and he says this is just a return to the tax jungle of the thirties. Well, we seem to be returning to the thirties in a great many ways in the sixties, and this is just another example.
There is one very important question which arises. These reductions are to come into effect on January 1. That means that unless every provincial legislature in this country meets later this year and imposes additional taxes there will be a period early next year when the total tax will be lower. Then the provincial governments, in order to get revenue, will have to increase their taxes and incur that onus because of this totally unnecessary and totally retrograde measure and because of the repudiation of the word given by this government to the premiers. The result is that we are going to have confusion, we are going to have a tax jungle, and we are going to see a great deal of unnecessary public misunderstanding.
Let no hon. gentleman on the other side say the government is decentralizing and returning to the provinces their rights. The provinces have always had their rights. The province of Quebec exercised its right and still exercises this right. One respects them for doing this, because they want to do it that way. But surely, when the government of Newfoundland and the government of Nova Scotia, the government of New Brunswick and the government of Manitoba do not want to have to go to the expense, trouble and annoyance of having a separate income tax and) are quite satisfied with the arrangements which have brought order into our national finances out of the chaos which Mr. Mackenzie King found when he came into office in 1935, the government of the day should not be considering so retrograde a step as this. Surely, this is a terrible thing to be doing now-to try to plunge this country, and particularly the poorer provinces, back into that chaos from which the wise and courageous policies of the Liberal government have carried us in the years between 1945 and 1957. We had reached the point where even the intransigent premier of Quebec, the late Maurice Duplessis, said, after the system of equalization was substituted for the system of tax rentals four and a half years ago, "It is still not what I want, but it is much better than anything we have ever had before." He said that, and, what is more, he took the money. He took the money and he was very glad to get it, because if he had not taken it the province would have been bankrupt. Those are the facts. They are incontrovertible, and notwithstanding the money which the province took in those last few years the pro-

vincial treasury was more or less bankrupt when, finally, his successors were defeated.
I say this is a retrograde step. It is a repudiation of the principle of equalization which has brought order into our national finances and into federal-provincial relations. This alone, if there were nothing else in this bill, would merit condemnation of this measure.

Members of the C.C.F. group over the years have been strong supporters of federal-provincial tax agreements and the equalization which has flowed therefrom. We feel that the tax agreements, if continued, will enable the federal government to cooperate with the provinces to bring a greater measure of equality into the financial resources of the various provinces which make up our country.
We think this is a backward step. We think the government has not endeavoured in any way to get taxation agreements as heretofore but has gone to the provinces on a take it or leave it basis. The government, by this measure, is saying that it is ceasing to discuss with the provinces any alternative proposals. The premier of Saskatchewan, in correspondence with the Prime Minister, has asked that before a measure of this kind is undertaken there should be another federal-provincial conference-a final conference as he put it- to deal with the matter, the precedent for this being the 1956 arrangement of the St. Laurent government.
We are being asked to pass this particular clause before having had a general debate on federal-provincial financial agreements. We think this is putting the cart before the horse. We should have had an opportunity to debate the general agreements before being presented with this measure which, when passed, will be a fait accompli. It will mean that the provinces have no alternative but to accept it and that the debate on the general taxation agreements will take place after the government and parliament have committed themselves to a particular course.
We think this measure demonstrates that federal-provincial relations in Canada are at an all-time low. The provinces across this country have registered many objections to a proposal of this kind. The province of Ontario will, of course, be placed in a position to make a substantial gain, but the whole principle of equalization is being repudiated. People in certain provinces will have definite advantages, but the principle of equalization has gone down the drain.
Mr. Chairman, we shall have further speeches to make when we are on the resolution itself, but we state now that this is a retrograde, a backward step.
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, I am wondering what allocation will be made of this income tax to the provinces. I refer to a taxpayer who might live in one province and earn his living in another. Subclause (3) of clause 13 appearing at page 9 of the bill says "income earned in the taxation year in a province". Should that read "in the province", or what is the meaning of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, so far as this clause of the bill is concerned, we are dealing here with income that is subject to federal taxation. For this purpose it does not matter in which province the money is earned. The matter determining the time and place of the earning of the income as among the provinces is something we will be dealing with in another connection.
So far as this particular clause is concerned we start with federal tax, and there is provision for a reduction corresponding to the kind of abatement we have under the present tax rental system. It will be available in the case where the income is earned in the taxation year in a province, the purpose being to enable the provinces-those which wish to do so-to legislate for the purpose of applying a provincial income tax on the said income.

Mr. Chairman, I have been told and I have learned on more than one occasion that the longer one is a member of parliament the less one should be amazed at what goes on. I must say I am somewhat astounded that we should now be discussing a clause such as clause 13 of Bill No. C-120. I have learned from reading clause 13 and the explanatory note what the minister has in mind, and I say bluntly that I think it is the height of audacity, hypocrisy and impudence for us to have before us now a proposed taxation change before we have discussed the principles of the resolution dealing with new dominion-provincial fiscal arrangements. Surely, Mr. Chairman, the procedure is to pass the principles first and then to proceed with the arrangements. This fiscal policy began in 1941 and continues until the end of March next year. A change is proposed in the contractual basis of the fiscal arrangements which surely should be made before we actually deal with the Income Tax Act, this week, next week, or at some future time. In other words, this is accepted now as a fait accompli without our having discussed the principles of the new agreement. I say that is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with all respect, the hon. member is mistaken. That point was discussed earlier. The house gave approval to the principle of this

Income Tax Act
bill in adopting second reading at noon today. We are now in the committee stage dealing with the clauses of the bill. There is on the order paper a resolution dealing with the proposed federal-provincial fiscal proposals for the ensuing five years. I hope we will be discussing that very shortly. I intend to make a statement in regard to that subject as soon as the item is called.
By this bill we are simply carrying out an undertaking given to the provinces. The provincial governments all understand that they will have to call sessions of their legislatures this fall in order to enact the necessary legislation, and it is highly desirable that the provincial governments know precisely what parliament has enacted. There is no question here of jumping the gun or anything of that kind. There will be a full opportunity to discuss the principles of that proposed federal-provincial proposal. The principle of this bill was approved today by the house when second reading was given and it was referred to the committee.
1 understand that, Mr. Chairman, but I say that the basic principle of this clause is dependent upon the passage of that resolution and the resulting bill which we still have not before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is well aware that under the existing system legislated under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act there is provision for abatement in the case of a province which chooses to collect its own personal or corporation tax. The provision contained in clause 13 is the counterpart of that kind of abatement. It provides for the counterpart of that kind of abatement which will exist under the proposed new system.
It is dependent upon the other bill being passed, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member is attempting to preserve his right to discuss the other measure fully, I might say that by the adoption of this clause his right to debate or discuss the other measure will not be abridged at all. Parliament can approve this provision and still decide not to approve the other resolution. It is dependent upon the will of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, clause 13 deals with income tax arrangements. Where is a reference to that to be found in this bill? Where is there any reference to corporation taxes, because that too is involved in the arrangements between the federal and provincial governments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we will be dealing with that subject when we reach clause 19 appearing at page 12.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, does the minister realize that if he continues the formula he is now putting forward, by the year 2046 we will no longer be in this field?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This provision runs up to and includes the year 1966.
Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief. Was the hon. member for Welland rising?
Get up and get on with it.

Mr. Chairman, I intended to pursue very briefly the question which the hon. member for Welland asked in respect to which the minister suggested it could be settled effectively when the other measure is before us. Surely these abatements which are laid down in this bill are going to be based on some appreciation of what province the tax is attributed to. I suggest there are going to be problems in this context. The federal parliament can say what its view is as to whether the income is earned in Quebec or in Ontario-that is taxable in Quebec or Ontario-but so long as the legislature of Quebec or Ontario puts on a direct tax, it can be put on any basis it likes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It still has to be constitutional.

Yes, but the province can put on a direct tax in respect to anyone subject to its jurisdiction. There is no question whatever about that. It does seem to me that although it will not be as great in the case of individuals as in the case of corporations it is going to be a real problem in the determination of how much of the federal tax was in fact collected from taxpayers in Quebec, how much from taxpayers in Nova Scotia, how much from taxpayers in Ontario, so as to know what the value of the-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is not a new
problem. We have that problem today. There are two provinces which collect taxes wholly or in part. This problem is not a new one.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in respect to this matter, the minister seems not to have dealt with the charge made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, that this was an attack on the principle of equalization. I should like to confirm what the hon. member has said by putting a statement on the record to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The fact is this does not touch that matter at all.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It does.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With respect to the hon. member, no.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the minister allow me to complete what I have to say and perhaps he could then comment on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is really out of order here; it does not apply to this clause at all.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not out of order here. You say clearly that this new section provides for a reduction of the personal income tax for the years 1962 to 1966, inclusive, in accordance with new fiscal arrangements with the provinces commencing on April 1, 1962. Therefore there is of necessity a reference to the fiscal arrangements made between the federal government and the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not the equalization; this has nothing to do with that.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It has been said that the principle of equalization has been abandoned and I simply wish to confirm that by reading a statement made by the premier of Quebec following the last meeting which took place and which is reported in the Ottawa Citizen of February 25, 1961 in an article entitled:
Premiers' reaction mixed to P.M.'s new tax proposal
This is the statement:
The equalization formula, of which Quebec is currently the biggest beneficiary, has been changed in such a way that it is no help either. Not until the fourth or fifth year of the new tax-sharing agreement, by finance minister Fleming's estimate, will the government of Quebec qualify for anything more than the guaranteed floor equalization payment.
On the same subject the Toronto Globe and Mail of February 24 carried an article under the heading:
Lesage calls plan smokescreen
The article reads in part as follows:
"We are offered a so-called national formula which is applicable only to Ontario," he said.
This is the premier of Quebec speaking: I continue:

It seems to me that this is not a matter that can quite be left in the nonchalant manner in which the minister has left it. It seems to me that the minister has either said too much or too little. The minister has told us that the premier of Quebec asked not to have continued this provision that was made last year. Surely this is a very important matter that is involved here. If we adopt this clause we are dropping a provision for which the minister took credit to himself a year ago and which would put the people of Quebec on a basis of equality with those in the other provinces; and he was very scornful of the attitude we took on this side of the house about this matter. He said he had solved this problem that the Liberals had been unable to solve. He boasted a great deal about that solution. Now he comes before us and just drops his solution and expects the House of Commons to regard this as a matter of no consequence or of no moment. If the minister felt as he said he did a couple of years ago, I cannot understand what is being done now?
We all remember his eloquent speech with which I agreed. I do not often agree with the minister but I agreed with that speech. He said it was intolerable, if that was his word; I have not the text of his speech before me. However, in effect he said it was intolerable to have this money that was collected from all over Canada paid in two thirds of the country but not in the other third. I agree completely with that statement. I think the minister for once was showing himself to be broadminded and statesmanlike. The minister said he was going to solve that problem and he brought in a solution last year that he told us would solve that problem for all time. Now he is just quietly dropping his solution and giving us no explanation at all. If this problem was as urgent as the minister said it was two years ago-and I think it was; I agree with the minister about that matter and I said that previously-what has happened to make it less urgent now?
When one considers all the time that has been spent in the last year in carrying on these discussions with the province, I would have thought that the minister would have taken some initiative in seeking to discuss with the government of Quebec how this matter was to be arranged and, if this particular provision was to be dropped and this particular solution was to no longer be a solution, what solution is going to be found. Before we drop this legislation and change it I think we should know what has happened. After all, as the minister pointed out,

if Quebec does not want to go on being a prescribed province, it will not matter that it is in our law; they do not have to be a prescribed province. However, I do not think the minister should so quickly drop this statesmanlike solution he found a year ago-just drop it into the sea-without having anything whatever to put in its place. That procedure does not seem to be consonant with that statesmanlike attitude the minister adopted a year ago.
After all, I do not think there is anyone in the House of Commons who does not wish to see the people of Quebec receive in one fashion or another out of the federal treasury their fair share of the money collected from all over Canada that is to be used for the support of the universities. That is a general proposition and I think everyone agrees with it. There are in some provinces some people who attach no importance to the way in which that money is paid. They do not care how it is paid as long as they receive it. In other provinces there are people who do attach importance to the method by which the money is paid, and who consider that it is very important that it should be done in accord with what is their view of proper constitutional arrangements. I certainly respect their views in that matter. I respect them completely and I have always respected them. I do not say I have always understood all of them but I have always respected them.
However, for us here in this parliament just quietly to drop this provision, to have nothing to put in its place and to be told by the minister that he is doing this because the premier of Quebec asked him to do it but does not wish to say any more about it, seems to me to be a little bit less than frank with us. I think we ought to be told whether this was just a casual reference made in a casual conversation or whether the minister received a formal communication from the premier of the province or just what happened.; and whether, when this was received, any overtures were made to the provincial government with a view to finding some other solution to the problem or whether this was just another case in which the government, because it has an awkward problem, is going to try to forget about it.
It seems to me that we cannot allow this matter to rest where it is now and adopt this amendment which just throws away the fruits of the minister's statesmanship of only a year ago. I think the minister ought to tell us whether he has taken any steps to find out what would be a method acceptable to the present government of the province of Quebec for dealing with this problem. The minister was at great pains to deal with the previous government of Quebec; he was very

anxious; he was very concerned; he went out of his way. Surely the minister is not going to say that, because the political complexion of the government of Quebec has changed, his zeal for justice and for fairness that he had a year ago has evaporated all of a sudden. I cannot believe that of the minister. At any rate, I should be very reluctant to believe it. I should hope that the minister would be able to tell us that he is in active negotiation with the government of Quebec and that he believes he has a solution of this problem, if he has one; or if he has not, I think he ought to tell us what he has done about it. It is a very serious thing. If we are going to maintain unity in this country we in this parliament, regardless of party, must seek to treat all parts of the country equally and fairly. I would hate to see us go back to that regrettable situation-
Which you were in five years ago.

Yes, which we were in five years ago. That is right. It was a regrettable situation as the hon. gentleman knows well, because he follows matters of this kind very closely. The hon. member knows well why we were in that regrettable situation. When the Massey commission recommended the university grants in the first place they were established by the St. Laurent government. The hon. member for Greenwood recalls those events very well, because he pressed the St. Laurent government to do that. He expressed great appreciation of it when it was done and gave the warmest possible support to it. The first year after those grants were established the premier of Quebec accepted them. Perhaps I should not say that he accepted them, exactly, but he entered into an arrangement with the then minister of finance whereby they were accepted by the universities in Quebec for one year. Then, for reasons which those of us who are not privy to the mind of that gentleman have never been able to understand, what was perfectly acceptable one year became totally unacceptable the next year.
For several years the people of Quebec lost the benefit of these payments. Then, in an effort to find another solution, my right hon. friend, Mr. St. Laurent, back in 1956, I think it was, or 1957, found a method by which these grants would accumulate until such time as a means could be found to make use of them. In other words, notwithstanding the intransigence of the government of Quebec the government of Canada said: we must find a way to be just, and we will save up the money. Of course, we had money to save in those days. We did not have deficits. We said: We will save up the money until some 90205-6-493J

expressed. I make it quite clear that we are not terminating anything. The hon. member talks about our terminating something. We are not terminating anything. The minister did a lot of prejudging last year when he brought in his great statesmanlike solution to this problem. I wonder whether this situation has improved. I take full blame for the former situation, but what is happening now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This amendment concerns donations by charitable foundations to governments and municipalities. It arises out of budget resolution No. 4. The particular amendment has been requested to permit a foundation to make donations to a municipal agency such as an art gallery.

This amendment is interesting. Some of us are a bit credulous with respect to those who would donate on a charitable basis for the purposes referred to in the resolution and in the amending bill. What kind of offers have been made in this regard so far that would warrant this amendment to our income tax laws? Has the minister knowledge of offers that have been made by way of gift to Her Majesty in the right of Canada or a province or to a Canadian municipality? If so, has any substantial amount been involved in recent times?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is the matter sub judice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no litigation about this.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 22 carry?

The minister is proposing to parliament that we amend the Income Tax Act to provide that there will be clear tax-free protection for a donation by an otherwise taxable person if he is giving something to Her Majesty in the right of Canada or a province or to a Canadian municipality. Maybe I am naive but I am not aware of many people who do this kind of thing. Something must have prompted the Minister

Income Tax Act
of Finance to amend the Income Tax Act to provide that under such circumstances such a gift would have the tax advantages proposed in the bill.
I recall that the Minister of Finance rather looked askance at the attitude of a former administration which felt that they had received from one or two estates a very substantial tax advantage which might be diverted to unusual purposes for the advantage of the public. Here we are concerned with the matter of a gift by a taxpayer to a government. In the former case it was a matter of the government deciding that these were receipts rather unexpected and unanticipated in times of great prosperity when it might be possible to divert equivalent assets in another way to something like the Canada council. There was no thought on the part of taxpayers who were passing away that they were making a gift to Canada, to a province or to any other area of public ownership. This was fortuitous and accidental. I think we should know from the Minister of Finance what prompts him to suggest that an incentive could be granted to people who might, in a way in which I have never known about before, wish in the future to make an outright tax exempt gift to a government, whether federal, provincial or municipal. I am not quarrelling with that principle. However, I think we are entitled to information as to what has led up to this. Why does the minister recommend this? He has information that we in the opposition do not have.
If there are people who want to donate, in a taxation year, their income to a government agency such as the Canada Council, I think we should have information concerning that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have already said, Mr. Chairman, that this amendment was requested to permit a charitable foundation to make a donation to a municipal agency such as an art gallery. This provision is designed to remove any limitation in respect of gifts by such non-profit corporations or charitable foundations to Her Majesty in the right of Canada or a province or municipality, such as the particular occasion to which I have referred.

Have we, in the past, suffered by the absence of this amendment? If so, could the minister indicate under what circumstances we have suffered, perhaps, from the charitable inclinations of anybody in Canada because we did not have this proposal in the act before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I think all of us desire to encourage those who have wealth and who plan that this wealth, after their death, will be devoted to cultural and social purposes. We want to be sure that they have a full opportunity to do so. The minister referred to an individual foundation. There is just one observation I should like to make before the clause is carried. It must have been rather painful,
I would think, for the minister to put this clause in this particular language because what it does is to make Her Majesty a charity or, more particularly, to make the treasury of Canada a charity. In view of the present state of the treasury of Canada, I would have thought the minister would have been quite sensitive about doing that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is not a new
provision. There has been such a provision in this act for many years in relation to gifts to Her Majesty and these qualify for the purpose of reducing taxable income, Mr. Chairman. It was written in, as a matter of fact, in 1950.

Would the minister look at page 15, subclause (b) of subsection 4? I want to say that this perhaps worries me more than some other items in the clause to which I have referred. It says:
There shall be included in computing a corporation's income all gifts received by the corporation and all amounts contributed to the corporation to be used for scientific research.
I have already commended the minister for some of the amendments he has introduced in his budget in respect of scientific research. I am concerned about whether or not a gift would necessarily be, in layman's language, a gift of a capital nature. As I read this paragraph, once one of these research corporations has been established and I were to give it a gift of $100,000 in 1961, which I could not do, I take it that would be regarded as income in that year and 90 per cent of it would have to be spent in that year. Perhaps I would wish my gift to be regarded as a capital grant, and perhaps I would be more concerned about the interest on my capital grant over the years being used by this nonprofit research corporation, rather than have my gift regarded as income after the establishment of the corporation so that 90 per cent of it would have to be disbursed in that year. Am I wrong in my review of the amendments that are here?
I admire what the minister is doing here. He is encouraging corporations and individuals to invest in research. However, unless I misjudge the interpretation here, I question the requirement that 90 per cent of the funds received in a current year must be disbursed in that year. I wonder whether or not that requirement prevents a bona fide research corporation from receiving from anybody in Canada what is called here a gift, without the necessity that such gift be disbursed to the extent of 90 per cent in the year of receipt.

Before the minister replies, I wonder whether I might make a brief comment. First of all, I should like to commend the minister for bringing in this particular amendment covering scientific research. Many of us who serve on the research committee find it extremely encouraging that we have some tangible evidence of the government's interest in our operations and activities. When the minister is giving his reply I wonder whether he could indicate the scope of 90205-6-494

the definition of "scientific research". We in the research committee, perhaps loosely, have kept it to the one word "research". I wonder what effect the addition of the word "scientific" has. speechtext:
The expression "scientific research" is defined by the Income Tax Act, section 72, subsection 4,

Having given credit to the government for encouraging in a new and substantial way the devotion of funds for research that will sustain some acceleration owing to tax laws, may I say this. If we have set up a corporation that is in all the sense of the act a truly and wholly desirable nonprofit research corporation, I cannot see that we should legislate to say that any taxpayer who subsequently makes any gift-I think the word is "gift" in the section-to that very worthy corporation is, in making his gift, debarred from insisting that perhaps only the income of his gift rather than the capital would be included in income on the 90 per cent basis for the taxation year under consideration. I think this is an important matter. I have already commended the minister for his enterprise in this sphere. However, I think corporations will be established where the donor does not want necessarily to make a gift or, in fact, perhaps would not make a gift if he felt that 90 per cent of his gift had to be expended in the year following the gift. I think he would prefer that there were some continuation relative to his important capital donation. I wonder whether that result is what is defeated by these words.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

I simply predict that, whatever government is in power in a year or two-and I have some opinions upon that matter-this is legislation that will not likely stand. I do not think that people who have the kind of assets that we want to be devoted to this kind of worth-while entirely non-profit research enterprise are likely to make gifts-and I emphasize the word "gifts" -if the law says that those gifts must not be expended with relation to the return of the capital given to them but must be expended 90 per cent within the period of the taxation year within which the gift has been made. It is on this clause that the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska asked me about the contributions of employees to deferred profit sharing plans. I repeat that no provision is made for employees contributions to deferred profit sharing plans. The essence of such a plan is that the employer sets aside some portion of his profits not for immediate distribution among his employees but puts them in a fund. Into the fund he will make his payments periodically according to the provisions of the plan. The employee does not draw anything out until a stated period, presumably on retirement. Now, in the meantime benefits are accruing on his behalf in the fund, but under the legislation as it has been hitherto he was taxed in respect of the sums accruing to him under any such plan. Under the present amendments there will be a deferment of tax during the period when these sums are accumulating on behalf of the employee, and then when he retires and draws out benefits he will become taxable at that time on the benefits withdrawn.
There are extended provisions here dealing with the various aspects of the plan. We have the definition of the deferred profit sharing plan, what is meant by a profit sharing plan; and we have provisions for registration of such plans. The minister is not permitted to accept for registration any of these profit sharing plans unless they comply with a considerable number of conditions which occupy most of page 22 of the bill. Provision continues on page 23 for acceptance of such plans for registration by the minister. They are given a registration date, and no tax is to be levied under subclause 6 while the trust is governed by the plan.
Then there is provision in subsection 7 for setting a ceiling on the employer's contribution which may be deductible from his income for tax purposes, and here the ceiling is the lesser of either the aggregate of each payment paid by the employer in respect of the individual employee or $1,500 minus the amount, if any, that is deductible under another clause, so that we are working here broadly speaking under the same kind of ceiling as applies to registered pension plans. The employer, up to this ceiling of contributions, may deduct them from his income for tax purposes. In this way encouragement is given by the law to the establishment of deferred profit sharing plans.
Page 24 of the bill deals with the provision for limitation of deductions, the portion of receipts that are deductible, and page 25 deals with the appropriation of trust property by the employer and for the revocation of registration in the cases there stated. Page 26 of
[The Acting Chairman (Mr. McCleave).]
the bill sets forth the rules applicable to a plan that has been revoked.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River asked me earlier to deal with the differences between the provisions in this bill respecting deferred profit sharing plans and those in the 1960 draft bill. Perhaps I might review these briefly, if hon. members are interested in them, Mr. Chairman.
First, in regard to the definition of the plan, the present bill provides that the employer must join in the application to register a plan as a deferred profit sharing plan. In Bill No. C-84, which was the 1960 bill, only the trustee was required to make application.
Second, also in relation to the definition of the plan, the present bill deletes a restriction which existed in Bill No. C-84, where a plan covers the employees of more than one employer. In Bill No. C-84 contributions could be made only for the benefit of "employees of the employer or of a corporation with whom the employer does not deal at arm's length". The present bill provides that contributions may be made for the benefit of "emplo3'ees of that employer or employees of any other employer".
The third difference is in relation to withdrawals for cause. The present bill removes a restriction which existed in Bill No. C-84 concerning withdrawals from a plan. Bill No. C-84 provided that a plan could not permit a payment of proceeds to any employee or beneficiary, except for a reasonable cause, before death or retirement of the employee or the winding up of a plan. The present bill removes this restriction and will permit plans to pay out proceeds at any time to employees if they choose. Such proceeds will, of course, be taxed when received.
This change means that the Department of National Revenue officials will not have to judge what is "reasonable cause" for a payment under a plan. This decision will be left to those who manage the profit sharing plan.
The fourth difference relates to capital gains and losses. The present bill provides that net capital gains made by the trust while a plan was an employee's profit sharing plan may be received tax free when paid out as proceeds. This concession was not contained in Bill No. C-84.
Only capital gains, less capital losses, made while the plan was an employees profit sharing plan qualify for this concession. Proceeds from a deferred profit sharing plan attributable to capital gains made by the trust while the plan was a deferred profit sharing plan are not exempt. This is in conformity with the tax treatment of capital gains made by

the trust of a pension plan. If a taxpayer is to enjoy the benefit of tax deferral on income he must be prepared to pay tax on all the proceeds accumulated during the period the plan was a deferred profit sharing plan.
The fifth difference relates to the date of registration. This present bill is much less restrictive concerning the date of registration of a deferred profit sharing plan. It permits the date of registration to be the date of application or any later date specified by the applicants. Bill No. C-84 provided that a plan would be deemed to become registered as a deferred profit sharing plan on the first day of the year immediately following the year in which the application was made.
The sixth difference relates to income of the exempt trust. The present bill adds a requirement that the trust for a deferred profit sharing plan must receive 90 per cent of its income from sources in Canada. This is in conformity with a similar requirement introduced in the December supplementary budget for trusts for pension plans. This requirement did not exist in Bill No. C-84.
The seventh difference relates to the notice of revocation. This present bill requires that notice of revocation of the registration of a plan as a deferred profit sharing plan must be mailed to an employer of employees under the plan as well as to the trustee. Bill No. C-84 required only that notice be sent to a trustee under the plan.
