is all it can afford to lose out of its immediate revenue? I can see a point there. If profits are paid into a deferred fund of this kind and there is no limit upon it there is, conceivably going to be a greater loss to the revenue in the current year than the treasury would care to contemplate, though, after all, employers have to make profits for the shareholders, too, so perhaps it would not go to very great lengths. But is that the sole basis of the $1,500 a year or is there some other reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the same reason as prompted the former government to propose a limit of $1,500 in the case of a contribution to an employee's pension fund. There are two reasons. Obviously, one is so that there may not be substantial tax benefits going to persons with large incomes related to provisions of this kind, and the other is the extent to which it is fair to impose a burden on the treasury in aid of such a plan.

My curiosity is aroused because of other debates we have had about some senior officials whose pensions have come under discussion. Am I right in my assumption that in so far as individuals are concerned the highest amount that any individual may deduct from his gross salary in the course of a year for payment into a retirement pension plan is $1,500 a year? I believe crown corporations occasionally make profits. Some do not. The Canadian National Railways incurs substantial deficits. But should they make a profit they are obliged, I believe, to pay income tax. But they could not deduct in respect of any employee, including the president, on a tax deduction basis, more than $1,500 for any one of their employees. Is that the situation across the land?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Leaving out past service, the act at the present time allows a contribution of $1,500 by the employer to an employee pension plan and $1,500 by the employee. In the case of the registered retirement savings plan where you have one person contributing instead of the employer-employee combination the maximum contribution is $2,500 per anum.

Yes. We are thinking of the private enterprise annuity or whatever was made possible in 1957. But you cannot have both. When we provide, in our new law, section 79C and incorporate that into our income tax schedule, no taxpayer, and this includes the corporations, as an employer, and no individual as an employee will be able to take advantage of more than one of the sections. The $1,500 has to be taken up by the corporation in connection with the
pension scheme or a deferred profit sharing plan. In a similar way, an employee cannot deduct $1,500 as his contribution to a pension plan and an additional $1,500 with respect to deferred profit sharing plan. Am I right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right. You cannot do it twice. Contributions can be made to the two plans but no more than $1,500 per annum per employee may be deducted for tax purposes.

The minister told my hon. friend from Drummond-Arthabaska that there was no limit to the amount of profit which an employer could put into one of these schemes for immediate distribution in the same tax year. I think the minister gave as his reason for that the explanation that this was assimilable to wages and therefore it was taxable as personal income. It is conceivable, of course, that the tax on personal income would be at a much lower rate than the tax would be in connection with corporation income tax. The government has decided to restrict contributions to $1,500, and I am not arguing about that, because the minister and his officials have got to judge what the needs of the treasury are. I am not criticizing that at all; I am just noting it. Is there any evidence that there is any serious loss to the treasury in revenue from these profit sharing plans where the profits are distributed immediately, a loss substantial enough to make the government feel there should be a limit there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are no statistics kept on this, but I have no doubt the answer would be in the negative.

I trust that my suggestion regarding procedure will be adopted. I think my hon. friends on this side all concur in it. At least, I hope they do. My suggestion is that we should take the subclauses one by one. It would be understood that we would not go back to them. This is a long, complicated and involved clause. I think that if we are going to do our duty as the representatives of the taxpayers we ought to scrutinize the clause carefully. I have only one more question to ask on subclause 1. It is an important question. The minister may say it is referred to in a subsequent clause. If he does, that ends it as far as I am concerned.
The minister has to approve these plans. There is a trustee. Does this mean that some kind of supervision of these plans is envisaged by the federal government to make as sure as they can be that they are run in a competent manner and that the trustees behave as trustees should, or do the federal government consider this to be beyond their jurisdiction?

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Obviously, the Minister of National Revenue is mainly responsible for reviewing the plan submitted in order to determine whether under subsection 2 he should accept it for registration. Then, if we were to read further on in this bill we would see the conditions under which the minister may revoke the plan. This is to be found in subsection 13. Obviously this arrangement assumes a measure of supervision. I am not going to say it can amount to a detailed measure of supervision from year to year but obviously in order to discharge the burdens put upon him by this clause the Minister of National Revenue will have to undertake supervision in the manner indicated.

Is this supervision to be exercised merely by the tax collector or is there to be some measure of supervision by, say, the superintendent of insurance? What does the government envisage in this regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be the Minister of National Revenue.

What kind of staff would be envisaged for the purpose of doing this work? This is really important. It does seem to me that if we are going to allow these deferred trusts, these deferred profit sharing plans to be set up, there might be serious eventual losses to the treasury, in addition to the deferment of immediate revenue if the funds were to be dissipated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot say in detail what kind of section will be set up within the department or how it will be staffed to deal with this. There are provisions here, Mr. Chairman, that obviously lay certain duties upon the minister and when the bill comes into effect the minister will have to be responsible with the assistance of the civil service commission to make the staff provisions required to discharge the duties imposed upon him by the legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I should imagine that the same kind of persons and staff that the minister now uses for whatever supervision he may give to pension plans would be the obvious kind of persons to be engaged in this kind of activity. Does the minister consider that to be correct? I cannot imagine that the government is asking us to set up a plan of this kind without having thought out the administrative scheme carefully before doing so. Unfortunately, as we all regret, the Minister of National Revenue is not here to give us any guidance in the matter. It might be that his parliamentary secretary could throw a flood of light on this question. He is here and we all know how

eager he is, and I am sure we would be delighted if he could give us a little help in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is nothing I can add to what I have said. This matter has to be worked out when the legislation is passed. It is partly a departmental responsibility and partly the responsibility of the civil service commission.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has a good point. We are enlarging the field under which some form of old age security may be worked out. We are referring now to a matter of deferred profit sharing which will be used, for the most part, by individuals for purposes of old age retirement. The minister came before parliament on budget night and talked about the portability of pensions as reported at page 6660 of Hansard of June 20, 1961. He also indicated his willingness to confer with the different provinces in regard to these matters. I was surprised that he indicated some insecurity in regard to pension schemes which already exist for old age retirement plans; yet at the same time he introduced, through tax laws, an element of encouragement in profit sharing which will take place under this proposed amending bill. He suggested there was some form of registration in existence now carried out by the Department of National Revenue.
I suggest we forget about the uncertainties that have existed in the past in regard to portability of pensions, because we are starting afresh this year with something which I assume the minister wants to launch on a sound basis. How does he intend to ensure that these new schemes will be registered and tied up with the Department of National Revenue? How does he intend to ensure that this program will be commenced on a clear and sound basis so that in future years we will not find it necessary to come back and discuss this scheme and its security with the provinces and companies involved? I suggest that is what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was dealing with.
We have exempted in a similar way contributions made by employers and employees to pension schemes. For a long time we have had very loosely defined registration of such schemes with the Department of National Revenue. However, in regard to this new type of tax exemption encouragement to individuals to provide security in old age by way of profit sharing plans, we are commencing under the aegis of the federal government something new which we hope will do the complete job. The minister has cast doubts upon a great number of old age security

Income Tax Act
schemes, payments to which are now exempted taxation and took a whole page of Hansard on June 20, 1961, to do so. Is he sure that this scheme is to be launched on a sound basis so that within three, five or 10 years it will not be necessary to come back to the companies, provinces and others to renegotiate it again? I think this type of assurance should be given by the minister because he said in his budget speech he intended to review the whole situation in regard to pensions, portable and otherwise.
I should also like the minister to deal with the portability of pensions provided by profit sharing programs. Is there any clause to be included in such schemes which would not allow an employee to benefit from years of employment until he had remained a certain period of time with a specific employer? Has that situation been taken into consideration in the drafting of the provisions now before us about which the minister boasts? Before he retracts some of the old plans which he has criticized I should like him to give some assurance that this new profit sharing arrangement provided for under this new measure-of which I approve and think very desirable-is being commenced on a proper and worth-while basis following complete and thorough consultation with the provinces, companies and others. I suggest in this regard the minister should give us an indication that he is going to be as paternal as he proposed he was in respect to the original plan for old age security to which he referred as reported at page 6660 of Hansard for June 20, 1961.
(Translation):
I would have another question to direct to the minister. Are the profits of a trust company, administering a pension fund for a group of workers, taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I did not understand the question.
I am asking the minister whether the profits of a trust company, administering a pension fund, are taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, it is a taxable profit.

I believe there is a section in the present act which says that the profits of a trust company are not taxable.
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the hon. member is misleading himself in talking all the time about a trust company. What he means is a trust fund. I am trying to read
some sense into his question. I think he means a trust fund or what is earned by a trust fund.
By the trustee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, by the fund. It is in the hands of a trustee. It is dealt with here. We will come to that.
It is not in this clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

I still have a question about the first subclause, or perhaps I should say an observation which follows the observation made so eloquently by my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River. It does seem to me, sir, that we have had about enough in this present year of those broad general principles enunciated by this government which at some time in the remote future are going to provide the administrative or regulatory framework for carrying them out. I will illustrate what I mean. This is just by way of analogy, sir; I am not seeking to debate this matter. Last November we were told we were going to have financial assistance for shipbuilding. We were told about it again in May, and a strategic moment in May, and we have been trying ever since to find out what the scheme is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Order.

This is just by way of analogy to show that we are being given the same old treatment here in this bill.
I said to the minister these deferred profit sharing plans have to be registered and there has to be a trustee prescribed who must make application in a prescribed manner. I asked him something about the degree of supervision and what facilities the department had for doing this. I asked him whether the same people would do it, or people similar to those who were now supervising pension plans with which, as my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River rightly reminded us, the government was not very well satisfied because the minister raised a good deal of questioning about the trustees of many of those pension plans. I believe that my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River was quite right in saying, if those pension plans have not been well supervised, if we are now going to start this new deferred profit sharing business, let us start it right, let us not have to come back, three, four or five years hence and say many of those trustees under this plan are not very satisfactory and we ought to be doing something about it.
This government seems to have vague, general ideas which it brings in in the form of legislation, with all kinds of regulatory power left to the governor in council to be

Income Tax Act
carried out some time after and it is usually some time after; but, sir, surely if this is going to amount to anything, if it is going to have any importance, the government ought to know now, and ought to have ready now, the regulations which are going to govern. I do not say that they can lay them on the table now; I am not asking that at all. But I am saying that in my experience when I was in the government-and I was in the government at one time and I had quite a lot to do with it for quite a long time-my right hon. friend, Mr. St. Laurent^ did not bring vague, nebulous schemes into this house. He knew where he was going and what he was doing and so did his ministers, and this is why in those days we had an administration in this country instead of a lot of nebulous ideas that never seem to come to any kind of fruition, or if they do they are shockingly badly administered.
From what the minister himself has confessed about pension funds it looks as though we are starting on the same road here with these things without any clear knowledge of how it is going to be done, without any knowledge whether the officials are there to do it.
I gave the hon. member for Edmonton West, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Revenue, the opportunity to tell us how this was going to be done. I am sure the hon. member is a very zealous parliamentary secretary. I am sure he knows. I am sure he has gone into this whole matter in the department and can tell us. I wish he would. I wish he would give us some reassurance as to how this job is going to be done and how efficiently it is going to be done. That is all I am asking. I do hope the parliamentary secretary will give us the benefit of the knowledge he undoubtedly has.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The question was answered some time ago. We are just getting a repetition of the question. The question has been answered. Would we not look bright, Mr. Chairman, coming here and saying we would set up a whole new section before the legislation was ever passed? We prefer to follow the constitutional manner, ask parliament to pass the legislation and then deal with the question of machinery and staff in a prescribed manner that will mean responsibility on the part of the department in association with the civil service commission.

I think I can answer that immediately by quoting the minister's words in his budget speech as reported at page 6660 of Hansard. He referred to what has been on the statute books for a long time and he took a good deal of our time on budget night

to say that in connection with pension plans he felt there was much that should be attended to. Now he is introducing something very controversial. I wish to refer him to his words. He said:
These pension plans are accorded valuable income tax concessions provided they are registered for this purpose with the Department of National Revenue. In general, tax deferral is granted during the period of accumulation and the pension benefits are taxed as personal income as and when they are received.
I doubt very much whether it is as well known as it should be that the federal government does not supervise or control the solvency of private pension funds; neither do the provinces.
The minister is introducing another form of tax exemption on exactly the same line after taking 20 minutes on June 20 to tell us, patting himself on the back, that he felt he was going to tidy up some of these matters for the benefit of those who might reach retirement age and expect to get financial benefits when they arrive at that age. But, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has said, he is introducing something new without in any way assuring us that he has provided for those concerned the kind of protection which he said on June 20 was desirable and which had been ignored in the past and which, in consultation with the provinces, he proposes to rectify. That is the position we are in.
What is the project? Is the degree of supervision of trustee plans in the public interest comparable in some respects with the supervision traditionally exercised over insurance companies? Many people may be surprised to learn that no such supervision has existed with respect to pension plans in the past. These are the words of the Minister of Finance when he is appealing to the public in his budget speech with respect to old fashioned ideas of savings provided not only by employers but matched by employees. Now with respect to this plan, when we are introducing new legislation, when the minister has all these things in his mind with respect to the past, why can he not tell us of the supervision which he points out was absent in so far as the federal government is concerned? What supervision does he expect to provide with respect to those deferred profit sharing plans? What reason is there for not telling us about the federal supervision at the time that this kind of legislation is being introduced? Inferentially at least the minister criticized in the past the fact that pension plans had some elements of danger connected with them and should be reviewed, and if he is introducing something new that involves tax exemption on both sides, employer and employee, why can he not say at the same time what he is going to do to make sure

that there is what he referred to as the supervision traditionally exercised over insurance companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a most unprofitable way to spend the time of this committee to engage in repetition of the kind we have been having. I have already dealt with this question.
I was giving you your own words. I thought you would like to hear them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member has given me my words about something entirely different and I wish he could get these two things clearly separated in his mind. In the one case we are dealing with deferred profit sharing plans and in the other we were dealing with pension plans. There are actuarial considerations applicable to pension plans that do not apply to deferred profit sharing plans because in the case of pension plans you have contributions by employers and employees. In the case of deferred profit sharing plans you have contributions made by employers. So you have a different situation altogether, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member can read the language of this clause quite clearly, I am sure, and see what is required in the way of decision, in the way of supervision on the part of the minister. The language of the clause is quite clear in the duties it lays upon the minister and you may be sure those duties will be discharged.

Mr. Chairman, after this lecture to the opposition-and we have had a good many from the minister about how wrong it is for us to repeat things that it seems to be very difficult for the minister to understand-may I say that the minister's idea of an answer in this house, which is all right under the rules on the orders of the day, of course, but is a very different thing when we are in committee, is to say "I answered that", and his original answer is usually to read the explanatory note or perhaps half of it.
I did not rise to comment on what the minister said this time so much as on what he said last time. His expression was, "Wouldn't we look bright?" Well, it would be pretty hard for them to look bright at any time in this year, I am telling you, and that is what the public is coming to see. He said, "Wouldn't we look bright if we had our plans ready to carry out this law when it is passed?"

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not what I said.

I suggest that the trouble with this government, as I have said before,
Income Tax Act
is that when they pass a law they have no idea how to administer it. The thing lies around for months and even years without anything being done about it because they do not think these things out in detail in advance. I can tell the minister that I was around here in the days at the end of the war-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The great I am.

-when the economy of this country was being transferred from a wartime to a peacetime economy and when Mr. Ilsley, Mr. Howe, Mr. Claxton, the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Laurier were piloting legislation through this house that gave the country the years of full employment we had up to 1957. When those things were happening we knew what we were going to do about the laws after they were passed. We did not start erecting an administration after the law had been passed.
I say that for the minister to say that he does not even know who is going to administer this, that he supposes they will get some civil servants and he supposes these civil servants will conduct some kind of supervision, and he does not know how extensive it will be, is to say that they would look bright if they knew. I think they would look bright if they knew and, to put it the way my children sometimes put it to me, I suggest it is about time they "smartened up".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Aren't you the bright fellow?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Your family must say that to you about three times a day.
Shall clause 26 carry?
No, we are still on subclause 1. For my part I would be quite prepared to have subclause 1 carried and we could go on now to subclause 2.

Is it
agreeable to the committee that we proceed through clause 26 subclause by subclause?
No.
Mr. Chairman, I would suggest-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely we can make some progress. Can it not be called a page at a time?
I think even the minister will agree with this suggestion. We are on subclause 2 of the clause 27, I take it.

They have now changed it to 26.

Income Tax Act
I know, but I cannot keep up with the amendments.

Order. I take it that it is agreeable that the committee proceed through this clause page by page. It will perhaps make it easier for the committee's deliberations. Shall the section of the clause on page 21 carry?

First of all, sir, in paragraph (a) of subclause 2 the plan provides that each payment made by an employer to a trustee in trust for the benefit of employees of that employer or employees of any other employer who are beneficiaries thereunder, is an amount that is the aggregate of amounts each of which is identifiable as a specified amount in respect of an individual employee. That is going to be prescribed as a condition of the plan but is there going to be some kind of continuous audit to see that in fact that provision is carried out? I would think it is very essential to the success of this plan that there should be some kind of audit in some kind of fashion to see that that does happen.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has, I think, not grasped the effect of this subsection. This is a term or condition of registration of the plan. The plan must make provision in the terms appearing in subsection (2) before the minister can accept the plan for registration.

But having accepted it for registration, is he not going to take any further interest? You can accept a plan for registration and then they can do something else entirely unless there is some kind of supervision from some quarter. What I am asking is, what kind of policing, what kind of auditing is going to be done to see that in fact the plan is carried out, or is none to be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member will look at page 26, subsection (13)(b) he will see that if any provision of the plan has not been complied with the minister may revoke the registration of the plan as of any date following the date that the plan ceased so to comply or that any provision of the plan was not so complied with, and he shall thereupon give notification of his action by registered mail to a trustee under the plan and to an employer of employees who are beneficiaries under the plan.

That is perfectly true but we have had long experience with what we call the blue book of registration of pension plans in the Department of National Revenue. I did not read this before; but I come back

to the minister's comments in the budget where he was very exuberant. He said:
There is, however, no governmental supervision to ensure that the assets of other plans are being accumulated at an appropriate rate to meet the future liabilities of those plans.
I know that the minister has said that the same liability does not exist with respect to profit sharing plans unless there is an appropriate deduction in compensation by the employee. I agree. However, I see nothing here to say that perhaps under some of these plans the employee is not going to be obliged to make a contribution and perhaps to buy stock in the corporation with which he is employed or in some of its other enterprises. The minister has complained of laxness over the years and he has introduced a new feature. I approve the new feature but I say that at the time of introduction surely the minister should present us with evidence that he is starting out to guard against the kind of thing that he complained about in connection with the availability of opportunities for old age security for employees. The minister said that there is no individual provision to assure that assets are being accumulated at an appropriate rate to meet future liabilities of these plans.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I repeat what I said earlier, Mr. Chairman, about the difference between deferred profit sharing plans and pension plans. The pension plan involves contributions by employers and employees under a contractual arrangement under which there is an undertaking to pay stipulated amounts on a periodical basis to the employee or pensioner at a particular time. Now that, of course, involves a question of the actuarial soundness of the plan. But in the case of deferred profit sharing plans, there is no contribution by the employee. There is no stipulation as to periodical payments. In this case it is simply a matter of carrying along and making available at the time of retirement the benefit of whatever amounts were paid in and credited to a particular employee. The particular employee will be taking some responsibility in relation to such plans himself. There is no contractual feature there in the sense that there is in a pension plan to give rise to the question of actuarial sufficiency.

Is the minister suggesting that under no circumstances will there be a profit sharing plan under which the employee makes contributions out of earnings that he could have taken as salary or compensation and that as an alternative he contributed to a profit sharing plan? In other words, is the minister suggesting that these amendments do not contemplate any scheme under which there would be a co-operative contribution,

perhaps on the part of the employer and employee, which would build up the employee's share in the deferred profit sharing plan?

It does not prohibit the employee from contributing but it offers no tax concession in such a case.
(Translation):

Under the present legislation, the beneficiary of a profit sharing plan is not required to pay income tax on the amounts he receives from the trust company, up to the amount of his own contributions. Nor is he required to pay tax on the capital gains of the trust. Under the amendment to the present act, I understand that these capital gains and contributions will be taxable. I should like to know why, under the amendment, capital gains and employee contributions will be taxable, whereas they were not under the present legislation?
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, is on page 27 or a later page, and not page 22.

I have one or two more questions concerning page 22. I was troubled by one observation made by the minister who went on to page 26 and said that if this condition that we set out for registration was not fulfilled, the minister could revoke the plan. Well, of course, I had read through the bill and I rwas aware of that. This was precisely what prompted me to ask the question that the minister seems to find so unintelligent when I ask it. My question was how the minister was going to find out if these conditions were being fulfilled. Does someone have to complain to him or will there, in fact, be some kind of continuous supervision?
There are a lot of detailed stipulations about these plans. I am sure the government is not putting them in there just for fun or in order to fill up the pages of the bill. I am sure the government must think there is some public interest to be served by putting them in here. If there is a public interest to be served by putting them in here, then there is a public interest to be served by seeing that they are fulfilled. I come back again to my question; what means is the government going to take to see that these conditions are fulfilled and are not merely part of a paper plan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member is evidently speaking about the conditions on page 22. Those are conditions on which the minister must satisfy himself before he registers the plan. Obviously, he must examine the plan with sufficient care to be able
Income Tax Act
to make the determination that is called for by each of the conditions prescribed in subsection (2).
Would the minister tell me why the second condition, (b), is a neces-ary one? It is not readily apparent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would not be a deferred plan if it were possible to borrow benefits out of it by way of a loan. If you allow loans to be made that is the very same thing as a distribution of the profits. The loans could be to the full amount of the employee's share of the profits. There has to be a deferment of the enjoyment of the benefit, Mr. Chairman, if there is a deferment of the tax.

The minister seems to have a rather different conception of a loan from the puritanical conception that I was brought up to have. My conception of a loan is something you pay back. It would appear to me that there would be no particular benefit if these employees used the deferred profits that were in this fund. Suppose an employee went to Household Finance and borrowed some money; that would not be regarded as a benefit that ought to be taxable. I should like to know what the reason is. After all, presumably any of these loans would be paid back. There probably is some good reason but the reason the minister gave is certainly not a good reason, unless the loans were not loans but were, in fact, just an indirect way of distributing profits immediately without any intention of recovering them and recovering them with interest.
It does not seem to me on the face of it that there is any more reason for a trustee not to invest this money in loans to employees, if they are good risks and if he can get a good rate of interest, than to invest in the minister's bonds or something else. As I say, there must be a good reason, but certainly it is not the reason given by the minister. I should like to know what it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have given the reason, Mr. Chairman. If the hon. member would read the provisions of the Income Tax Act he would see a good many other cases in this act in which provision is made to the effect that loans are to be treated as though they were a distribution and taxed as though they were payments out, to guard against cases where the provisions of the act would be avoided by people who take money out and call it a loan in the hope of evading tax on payments which, if they were called anything else but a loan, would become taxable as income. There are various provisions to that effect in the act.

Income Tax Act

The minister accuses me of not understanding the Income Tax Act, and in doing so he is quite right. I am not a careful student of the Income Tax Act. I thought I should like to take a sort of elementary course this evening. I think the minister cannot complain that my questions are not to the point. I never heard before about such provisions in connection with loans. I have once or twice had an overdraft at the bank, but I have never had to pay income tax on it. It is just possible that I might, at some time or other, have borrowed money from an employer, though mostly my employer has been the government of Canada or an impecunious university and they were not in a position to lend. This information that the Income Tax Act is studded with cases where loans are treated as income on which you have to pay a tax is news to me. I should like the minister to show me several examples because they may throw light on this situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think there is time in which to give the hon. member all the education he needs on this subject tonight. However, I ask that we stick to the clause under consideration. Perhaps then we could make a little progress. We have not passed anything now for about two hours.
We have not passed anything for the very good reason that this is an entirely new proposition-
The minister does not understand it.

-with which the minister is apparently so little familiar that he does not know how to explain it. I do not think that anybody anywhere, including the minister, believes the ridiculous explanation he gave for this provision, namely that if one of these funds lent money to the employee, that would be an indirect way of giving him an income. It is absurd; it is ridiculous. It may be that it is thought that they would not be careful enough. I can think of reasons myself, but I am not sponsoring this legislation. It is not my duty to explain it to the minister. I am a member of the opposition. As an opposition we have a duty to see to it that, as far as we can do so, silly, unnecessary or ill-conceived legislation or legislation that is not understood by the sponsor is not passed by this House of Commons. It seems to me that a plan of this sort is a good way in which to invest. After all, we think of credit unions which are not perhaps in many ways so very different from this. They exist for the very purpose of lending money to their members. Most of them have a very good

record of collections. I would think that the other persons participating in one of these deferred profit sharing plans would make it fairly unpleasant for any one employee who took money out on a loan and did not pay back the loan. I would have thought that on balance that this would be a fairly good way to invest the money, namely in loans to members. Section 79C, subsection 2(c) reads as follows:
(c) the plan provides that no part of the funds of the trust governed by the plan may be invested in notes, bonds, debentures or similar obligations of
(i)	an employer by whom payments are made in trust to a trustee under the plan for the benefit of beneficiaries thereunder, or
(ii)	a corporation with whom that employee does not deal at arm's length;
Will the minister explain what public or other interest is served by this particular stipulation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the purpose of this provision is quite obvious to all concerned. It is a question of solvency. It is a question of the direction of these moneys to the proper purpose. This plan is largely created by the employer through his contributions on behalf of the employee. That is the reason why this step is taken to prevent the funds of the plan from being used by the employer in his own business or in a business that is associated with his business.

I am speaking on subsection 2, and there are a number of subsections here. I felt the minister had not properly answered my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on an earlier question which related to loans. To bring something down to simple terms, if I were reading paragraph (e) of subsection 2 I would think it relates to loans. I would think it perhaps relates to a requirement by a person who may have all his assets in one of these deferred profit sharing plan schemes. He may have been so keen on participating that he does not even own his own home. He may have been a renter all his life. Everything may have gone into it. I have heard about one or two such people who have participated very successfully in the deferred profit sharing plan of their employer but to the extent that they have no current assets; they own practically nothing except perhaps a bit of furniture in their houses. Eventually they hope to share in the progress of the business in which they have been

employed. Under paragraph, (e) it is stated that this sole savings plan of the individual would not be available to him in the case of an emergency when he wanted to borrow some money and when he was in dire straits.
1 cannot think of anyone who was more eloquent in describing straits of this kind than was the Minister of Finance when again, on budget night, he referred to the extraordinary medical expenses which some of our people unfortunately are obliged to meet. He referred to a single motor accident. I quote from page 6661 of Hansard. As found there he stated as follows:
A single motor accident, for example, may cause a taxpayer more extraordinary medical expense in one year-
Order. I shall have to ask the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River how he relates this quotation to the material set forth on page 22 of this bill.

Mr. Chairman, I thought the minister had been so eloquent that I would use his words in order to indicate that a person having devoted all his resources and savings to one form of security at the time of retirement, namely that under a deferred profit sharing plan, might have no assets except his assets in the profit sharing plan. I am referring to paragraph (e) where it states that the minister would not accept for registration such plan if an individual in those dire straits felt obliged in any way to assign or surrender in whole or in part his assets and interest in this lifelong plan of savings through the profit sharing plan. That is why I referred to the catastrophe that could occur. I thought the minister on budget night had dealt with the matter very well when he said that today even one automobile accident might put a person who had not made other savings provisions into a position where he was in very dire straits.
Before we pass it, I ask what is the necessity for paragraph (e). In other words, this is a form of individual asset that has been accumulated over the years. In my illustration I take it that the man, if he went to his banker, could not point to anything except the fact that, all through his life, he had been a devoted servant to his company and that in consequence, in accordance with a plan they had with their employees, this company had provided for him a deferred profit sharing scheme. He needed money desperately. He had nothing. As a matter of fact, he may have been injured and in consequence may have had to terminate his employment. The question I ask is this. Why would he not be able to take recourse to the only asset he has, and perhaps a very consequential one, which had been accumulated

for him, and by his own design, in co-operation with his employer over the years? But it says here he could not suggest anybody who would lend him capital funds in this emergency-the kind of money he would need, say, for a temporary emergency.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Deferment of tax is a valuable benefit and it is associated with the deferment of payment. If you are going to allow benefits to be enjoyed during the period you are going to defeat the whole purpose of the relationship between deferment of benefit and deferment of tax.

With regard to paragraph (f) I have no particular query. It seems to me to be a sensible provision. As to paragraph (g) it is, of course, just the usual provision by the government to make as many regulations as possible which it had not thought of when the legislation was before the house. As far as subsection 2 is concerned, I should like to be able to say I am satisfied with the minister's explanation, but I think after the minister's total failure to give any explanation it is perhaps not much use for us to proceed further with it.

speechtext: I think the clause the hon. member is looking for is subsection (6). No tax is payable under this part by a trust on the taxable income of the trust for the period during which the trust was governed by a deferred profit sharing plan.

I confess I did not completely follow the question which my hon. friend asked in French, but long before this debate I had noted a question I wished to ask the minister with respect to subclause 3. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member
began with subsection 3 and has moved to subsection 4. Subsection 4 defines the registration date. On looking at subsection 3 it must be obvious to all hon. members that there are employees profit sharing plans in existence. tax concession must bring its capital gains into the fund up to date. Is that the point?
